issues.body:
## Summary

- **Motivation**
  - Long-loop rounds dropped from Exp1 (SFT 746 → RL 16: Micro `0.4526` / mean `0.5216`) to Exp2 (`0.4048 / 0.4829`) and Exp4 (`0.3763 / 0.4250`; #11337) while several SFT settings changed together.
  - Isolating which SFT knob drove the drop directly guides the Mochi SFT recipe.

- **Goal**
  - Identify which Exp1-to-Exp4 SFT setting change(s) account for lower general and agentic ability.

- **Data & Setup**
  - Base model: Snowball pre-trained base (`snowball-67b-a2b-base-262k-qk175-skew8`), fresh SFT, FP32-stored parameters (except Arm C).
  - Two SFT mixes:
    - **18 Nov mix:** used only for the initial LR and grad-clip screens.
    - **19 Nov / 6164 mix** (`20.47%` replay baseline, or `10%` in P1/P3): used for all other 1-hour and 8-hour arms.
  - Method: change one knob at a time at 1 hour (`150` updates), then validate decisive arms at 8 hours (`500` updates) on held-out loss, [edit-call](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/11536) (`1,197` items), and 14-clean-source Micro210 (two inference repeats).

- **Key Results (8-hour, step 500, 19 Nov / 6164 mix, `cw-rno2a`)**
  - **Expert banks on Adam — Arm E r2 (seed 0, `20.47%` replay) vs Muon-H control**
    - Held-out SFT loss: `0.4488` vs `0.5413`.
    - Micro210: **`57.70%`** vs `45.18%` (**`+12.52 pp`**).
    - Edit-call: intervals overlap (`0.825` vs `0.765` pooled applies). ([loss](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/11858#issuecomment-7078520306), [edit-call](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/11858#issuecomment-7080258692), [Micro210](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/11858#issuecomment-7081822894))
  - **Seed replicate — P2 (Adam banks, seed 2, `20.47%` replay)**
    - Held-out SFT loss: `0.4425`.
    - Micro210: **`50.56%`** (`+5.38 pp` over control, `-7.13 pp` vs seed 0).
    - Edit-call: overlapping (`0.782`). ([details](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/11858#issuecomment-7104658330))
  - **Adam banks + `10%` replay — P3 (seed 0)**
    - Lowest held-out SFT loss: **`0.4247`**.
    - Micro210: **`51.60%`** (`+6.42 pp` over control, `+1.04 pp` over P2, `-6.10 pp` vs seed-0 `20.47%`).
    - Edit-call: overlapping (`0.768`). ([details](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/11858#issuecomment-7104658330))
  - **RMSProp-style expert banks — Arm F (2nd moment only, no momentum, seed 0)**
    - Held-out SFT loss: `0.4433` (similar to Adam banks).
    - Sampled edit-call: `0.674` (below Arm E and control, non-overlapping intervals).
    - Micro210: `50.51%` (`-7.19 pp` vs Arm E r2; repeats overlap control).
    - Short 20-step Mochi Bank-RMS probes also failed the stability rule (`1.715x` twin loss, grad norm `218.67`). ([8h Arm F](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/11858#issuecomment-7087782018), [Mochi probes](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/11858#issuecomment-7080948760))

- **Conclusion**
  - Routing **4-D MoE expert banks to Adam** (keeping Muon-H on attention and 2-D/3-D matrices) is the dominant SFT lever at both 1 hour (`+24.99 pp` Micro210) and 8 hours (`+5.38` to `+12.52 pp` Micro210, ~`0.10–0.12` lower SFT loss).
  - Dropping momentum (RMSProp-style banks) matches SFT loss but trails on capabilities.
  - One training run per configuration; no causal claim is made.

Parent: #11535 · Related: #11337 (Snowball scoreboard), #11783 (replay sweep & Mochi results), #11793 (FP32 first-update hang).

🤖 **Scale difference from Exp1–Exp4 and Arm 1 dependency**

## Scale comparison

Our one-at-a-time SFT ablations run at 1/8th the per-update batch size of Exp1–Exp4:

| Setting | Exp1–Exp4 runs | Our 64-H100 ablations |
|---|---|---|
| Hardware | 32 hosts × 8 H100 (256 H100 in Exp1) | 8 hosts × 8 H100 (64 H100; mesh `context=8`, `data=8`) |
| Packed rows per update | 256 (`256 × 262,144` = 67,108,864 tokens) | 32 (`trainer.trainer.train_batch_size: 32`; `32 × 262,144` = 8,388,608 tokens, 1/8×) |
| Microbatch / accumulation | — | `gradient_accumulation_steps: 4` (4 microbatches of 8 rows scanned inside one update; loss divided by the full 32-row scored-token count, `_accumulated_loss_and_grads` at commit `3b291b10`) |
| Updates per run (`stop_after_steps`) | 204 (Exp2), 360 (Exp4), 388 (Exp3), 746 (Exp1) | 150 (one-hour size); 500 (8-hour size) |
| Raw tokens per run | 13.69 B (204 updates) to 50.06 B (746 updates) | 1.26 B (150 updates, 4,800 rows); 4.19 B (500 updates, 16,000 rows) |

Because both batch size per update (8×) and total trained tokens are smaller than Exp1–Exp4, effects that depend on batch size or longer training horizons may differ between the one-hour screen, the 8-hour screen, and 256-H100 scale.

## Arm 1 dependency

Arm 1 (changing stored parameter precision from BF16 to FP32 under Exp1's optimizer routing, with 4-D routed expert banks on Adam and stacked norm scales on Muon-H) waits on issue 11793 (first-update hang under that combination on the current long-loop runtime). Isolating optimizer routing on FP32 likewise waits on issue 11793, while the BF16 single-knob arms and an FP32 combined precision-plus-routing check do not hit issue 11793.

🤖

## Research

This is a multi-run experiment with no results yet. The historical comparison also changes RL duration (16 versus 36 updates), so SFT-only scores cannot by themselves explain the post-RL gap. [#11687](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/11687) documents the BF16 stored-parameter caveat in the Exp1-style baseline; [#11793](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/11793) blocks the FP32 plus Exp1-routing comparison on the current runtime. The Exp3/Exp4 supervision sidecar is hash-pinned in [`exp3_recipe.py`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/1be0454367925411db6a432da3f62901881f8152/experiments/post_training/long_loop/exp3_recipe.py#L114-L126), but its per-source loss modes still need to be checked against the intended mask arm.

## Plan

1. Freeze the pre-train checkpoint, 10/05 catalog, source-loss sidecar and hash, runtime revision, data order, update count, and evaluation policy. Inspect the sidecar's per-source modes and verify that each arm changes only its named setting. Split the proposed LR/betas/eps and packing-cap/lookahead arms; separate expert-bank and norm routing if those assignments can be varied independently.
2. Run a matched Exp1-style BF16 baseline and one-hour SFT screens with the same source weights, sampling seed, update count, and checkpoint steps. Record consumed token counts because packing and masking change them. Score each checkpoint on the same frozen Micro210 and edit-call evaluations. Repeat the baseline to measure run and evaluation variation before promoting an arm whose score change exceeds that spread.
3. Keep the FP32 plus Exp1-routing cell gated on #11793. Once update 1 completes reliably, run a matched precision × routing comparison, then take only the decisive settings to eight-hour, repeated SFT runs. Report both Micro aggregates, benchmark-level scores, coverage, edit-call scores, seeds, configs, and checkpoint links, including negative results.
4. For any SFT setting that plausibly explains the gap, continue a matched pair through the same RL recipe and number of updates. Compare the post-RL checkpoints under one evaluation policy before attributing any part of the Exp1-to-Exp4 post-RL difference to SFT.

comments.body:
🤖 **Optimizer routing per recipe: Exp1's expert banks fall through to Adam**

Source-verified parameter routing across five recipes (Exp1, Exp2, Exp3/Exp4 Hero-EP, the 11-19 control at `6164fcbd`, and the 10/05 run). No claim is made here about which routing performs better.

Conventions used below: `learning_rate` drives Muon-H and AdamH; `adam_lr` drives Adam. "Per-group" clip means `max_grad_norm` applied separately inside each optimizer group; "Global" means one gradient-norm clip across all parameters.

## Cross-recipe overview

| Weight group | Exp1 (`9662fdba02`, `bcf85728`) | Exp3 / Exp4 (`facbad18`) & 11-19 control (`6164fcbd`, `1f9bb1af`) | Real 10/05 (`ce7c77a`, `11baea1f`) | Exp2 (`442bf9d878`, `AdamConfig`) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Expert banks (`w_gate`, `w_up`, `w_down`)** | **Adam** (4-D fall-through) | Muon-H | Muon-H | Adam |
| Attention & shared-expert matrices | Muon-H | Muon-H | Muon-H | Adam |
| Gated norms | Muon-H | Muon-H | Muon-H | Adam |
| Stacked per-layer RMSNorm scales `(L, D)` | **Muon-H** (2-D match; no norm rule) | Adam | Adam | Adam |
| `embed_norm` / `final_norm` scales (1-D) | Adam | Adam | Adam | Adam |
| `output_proj` / LM head | AdamH | AdamH | AdamH | Adam |
| `token_embed`, `router`, `router_bias`, `attn_gate` | Adam | Adam | Adam | Adam |
| Clipping | none | global 1.0 | none | global 1.0 |

Every recipe except Exp2 uses mixed routing, with `token_embed`, `router`, `router_bias`, `attn_gate`, and `output_proj` routed the same way across all mixed recipes; Exp2 is the only recipe applying plain Adam uniformly to all parameters.

## Per-recipe routing tables (verified from source)

### (a) Exp1 (`9662fdba02`)

Optimizer `grug_moe_muonh_v1`, blob `bcf85728`; mask at `experiments/grug/moe/optimizer.py:285-307`. The SFT runtime stacks transformer blocks (`Transformer.stacked_blocks: ArrayStacked[Block]`, `sft_runtime/model.py:1251, 1283`), turning `(E, D, I)` expert weights (`levanter/grug/grug_moe.py:389-392`) into 4-D `(L, E, D, I)` leaves.

| Group | Optimizer | LR field | Clip |
|---|---|---|---|
| `token_embed`, `router`, `router_bias`, `attn_gate` | Adam (`L291-297`) | `adam_lr` `5e-5` | none |
| `output_proj` (LM head) | AdamH (`L298-299`) | `learning_rate` `5e-5` | none |
| gated norms (`embed`, `attn`, `mlp`, `final`) | Muon-H (`L301-302`) | `learning_rate` | none |
| attention `w_q/k/v/o`, shared expert `w_*`, latent `w_*` (stacked 3-D) | Muon-H (`L303-304`) | `learning_rate` | none |
| **expert banks `w_gate`/`w_up`/`w_down` (4-D)** | **Adam** (`L305` fall-through) | **`adam_lr`** | none |
| stacked RMSNorm scales `(L, D)` (2-D) | **Muon-H** (`L303-304`; no norm rule in this blob) | `learning_rate` | none |
| `embed_norm` and `final_norm` scales (1-D) | Adam (`L305`) | `adam_lr` | none |

`max_grad_norm: null` (`sft.yaml:75`) and blob `bcf85728` has no global clip option. Both `learning_rate` and `adam_lr` are `5e-5` (`sft.yaml:61, 73`), so the Adam fall-through changed the update rule for expert banks without changing their LR value.

### (b) Exp3 / Exp4 Hero-EP (blob `facbad18`)

Optimizer `grug_moe_hero_ep_muonh_v1`; mask at `moe_hero_ep/optimizer.py:308-327`.

| Group | Optimizer | LR field | Clip |
|---|---|---|---|
| `token_embed`, `router_bias`, `.attn_gate`, `.router` | Adam (`L314-315`) | `adam_lr = 5e-5 * 3/13 = 1.1538e-5` | global 1.0 |
| `output_proj` / `lm_head` | AdamH (`L316-317`) | `learning_rate` `5e-5` | global 1.0 |
| gated norms | Muon-H (`L319-320`) | `learning_rate` | global 1.0 |
| any `.weight` (RMSNorm scales, ShortConv) | Adam (`L323-324`) | `adam_lr` | global 1.0 |
| expert banks (4-D) and other 2/3-D matrices | Muon-H (`L325-326`; normalised per expert bank via `expert_normalization`, `L86-92`) | `learning_rate` | global 1.0 |

Per-group `max_grad_norm` is `None`. Global `1.0` clipping is set outside the optimizer (`global_gradient_clip=1`, `exp3_recipe:138`) and applied in `train_lm.py:328-329`.

### (c) 11-19 control (`6164fcbd`)

Optimizer `grug_moe_muonh_v1`, blob `1f9bb1af`; mask at `experiments/grug/moe/optimizer.py:339-363`.

| Group | Optimizer | LR field | Clip |
|---|---|---|---|
| `token_embed`, `router_bias`, `.attn_gate`, `.router` | Adam (`L345-351`) | `adam_lr` `2e-5` | global 1.0 |
| `output_proj` / `lm_head` | AdamH (`L352-353`) | `learning_rate` `2e-5` | global 1.0 |
| gated norms | Muon-H (`L355-356`) | `learning_rate` | global 1.0 |
| `.weight` (norm scales) | Adam (`L357-358`) | `adam_lr` | global 1.0 |
| 2/3/4-D matrices incl. expert banks | Muon-H (`L359-360`; 4-D banks use the hero backend with `expert_normalization: all_experts`, `use_syrk: true`, build `L263-297`) | `learning_rate` | global 1.0 |

Clipping comes from `global_grad_norm: 1.0` applied once before all groups (`L329-337`); per-group `max_grad_norm` is `null`. Routing matches Hero-EP `(b)`, and both use `expert_normalization: all_experts` and `use_syrk: true` (`moe_hero_ep/optimizer.py:228, 230` defaults in Exp3/Exp4); they differ in LRs (`learning_rate` `2e-5` vs `5e-5`; `adam_lr` `2e-5` vs `1.1538e-5`), with `1f9bb1af` sending 4-D leaves through the hero backend and 2/3-D leaves through the generic backend.

### (d) Real 10/05 run (`ce7c77a`, HF model card revision `8c76b22a`)

Trainer `experiments/grug_sft/special_token_lr.py` (`use_array_stacked_blocks=True` at `L334`); optimizer `experiments/june_tpu_67b_a2b/moe/optimizer.py` `GrugMoeMuonHConfig` (blob `11baea1f`, not `bcf85728`).

| Group | Optimizer | LR field | Clip |
|---|---|---|---|
| `token_embed`, `router_bias`, `.attn_gate`, `.router` | Adam (`L306-312`) | `adam_lr` `5e-5` | none |
| `output_proj` / `lm_head` | AdamH (`L313-314`) | `learning_rate` `5e-5` | none |
| stacked `rms_attn` / `rms_mlp` scales | Adam (`L317-318`, `rmsnorm_to_adam=True`) | `adam_lr` | none |
| gated norms | Muon-H (`L320-321`) | `learning_rate` | none |
| 2/3/4-D matrices incl. **expert banks** | **Muon-H** (`L328-329`) | `learning_rate` | none |

Config sets `learning_rate=5e-5`, `adam_lr=5e-5`, `max_grad_norm=None` (`special_token_lr.py:361-373`) with no global clip. One extra rule scales updates to the 7 special-token rows of `token_embed` and `output_proj` by `×√32` after the optimizer (`special_token_train.py:498-505`).

### (e) Exp2 (`442bf9d878`)

Plain Levanter `AdamConfig` (`levanter/optim/config.py:503-535`) with a single group (no mask, no `multi_transform`): every parameter gets `clip_by_global_norm(1.0)`, then `scale_by_adam`, then `lr = 5e-5`. Weight decay is `0`, so the decay mask is unused.

## Evidence that Exp1's 4-D expert-bank fall-through was unintended

- **Docstring mismatch:** The same blob `bcf85728` lists `"MoE MLP"` under `muonh` (`experiments/grug/moe/optimizer.py:215`).
- **`(2, 3)` rule vs. stacked 4-D banks:** The `ndim in (2, 3)` rule was written for the `grug/moe` template (`grug/moe/model.py`, `blocks: tuple[Block, ...]`), where expert weights are 3-D and match Muon-H. `sft_runtime/model.py` stacks blocks into `ArrayStacked[Block]`, making expert banks 4-D, and the mask in `bcf85728` was not updated for 4-D leaves.
- **Explicit 10/05 comment:** The 10/05 optimizer (`experiments/june_tpu_67b_a2b/moe/optimizer.py:322-327`, blob `11baea1f`) explicitly guards against this trap: *"plus 4D when use_array_stacked_blocks=True… Without including 4D, stacked expert weights fall through to adam"*.
- **Branch fix not in `main`:** Commit `02c96d8378` (2026-11-17, `"[grug] Preserve Muon state across expert routing"`, no commit message body) adds 4-D routing, the `.weight` → Adam rule, and `test_muonh_groups_match_hero_for_stacked_and_unstacked_models`. It is present in `6164fcbd` but **not in `main`**.
- **Still in `origin/main`:** `origin/main` (blob `81304114`, `L311`) still checks `ndim in (2, 3)`, so any stacked-block run on `main` using `grug_moe_muonh_v1` repeats Exp1's routing (which current recipes on `main` use it was not checked).
- Nothing found in source records the Exp1 fall-through routing as a deliberate choice.

## What Exp1 → Exp3 changed in optimizer routing

Moving from Exp1 (`bcf85728`) to Exp3 (`facbad18`) changed three optimizer behaviors together:

1. **Expert banks (`w_gate`/`w_up`/`w_down`):** Adam → Muon-H (with per-expert-bank `expert_normalization`).
2. **Stacked per-layer RMSNorm scales `(L, D)`:** Muon-H → Adam (via the `.weight` rule, and at `adam_lr = 1.1538e-5` instead of `5e-5`).
3. **Gradient clipping:** none → global norm clip `1.0` (`global_gradient_clip=1` in `exp3_recipe:138`, applied in `train_lm.py:328-329`).

## Unverified detail

How generic Muon (`_grug_scale_with_muon`) handles Exp1's stacked `(L, D)` RMSNorm scales was **not traced or verified**. As a 2-D leaf they may be orthogonalised across layers as a single matrix, so that behavior is left open rather than stated as fact.

## Open question for experiment owners

Was Adam on the 4-D expert banks (and Muon-H on stacked RMSNorm scales) in Exp1 intended, or an unintended result of stacking blocks under the `ndim in (2, 3)` rule?

## Held-out loss: LR 5e-5 with and without clipping (18 Nov recipe, one hour)

**Held-out loss, 18 Nov eager recipe, step 150: LR 5e-5 without clipping, against LR 5e-5 with clip 1.0 and the control at LR 2e-5.** All three arms are H100, BF16-stored (18 Nov baseline: expert banks on Adam, norm scales on Muon-H; see issue 11858), with the same 20.47% replay map (identical `data.train_weights`), linear schedule, no warmup and min_lr_ratio 0.1. The no-clip run differs from the clip run only in `max_grad_norm` (1.0 → None) and the cluster (cw-us-east-02a → cw-rno2a). Lower is better.

| set | control (LR 2e-5) | LR 5e-5, clip 1.0 | LR 5e-5, no clip | no clip − control | no clip − clip 1.0 |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| all (`eval/loss`) | 0.6115 | 0.6103 | 0.6070 | -0.0045 | -0.0033 |
| SFT (`eval/sft/loss`) | 0.5093 | 0.5022 | 0.4978 | -0.0114 | -0.0044 |
| SFT source macro | 0.5368 | 0.5299 | 0.5253 | -0.0116 | -0.0046 |
| replay pretrain (`eval/replay/loss`) | 0.8514 | 0.8639 | 0.8631 | +0.0117 | -0.0008 |
| pretrain c13q3 | 0.3489 | 0.3551 | 0.3509 | +0.0020 | -0.0043 |
| pretrain c28q4 | 0.5498 | 0.5552 | 0.5557 | +0.0059 | +0.0005 |

| SFT nemotron_sft_v3 macro | 0.5057 | 0.4778 | 0.4779 | -0.0278 | +0.0001 |

**Did clipping act, and do the two training curves match?** Read from W&B for both LR 5e-5 runs (150 updates each).

| question | clip 1.0 run | no-clip run |
|---|---|---|
| updates with a pre-clip total grad norm above 1.0 | 17 of 150 (updates 1-10, 13, 28, 31, 71, 101, 117, 144) | 18 of 150 |
| largest pre-clip total grad norm | 4.81 (update 2) | 9.19 (update 79) |
| median pre-clip total grad norm | 0.433 | 0.427 |
| updates where clipping changed the update (a group norm above 1.0) | 14 of 150 (updates 1-7, 9, 10, 13, 71, 101, 117, 144) | none (no clip) |
| train loss, update 150 | 0.4726 | 0.4727 |
| train loss, mean of updates 141-150 | 0.6721 | 0.6721 |

- **How clipping works here:** the optimizer (`grug_moe_muonh_v1`) clips each of its three parameter groups to norm 1.0 separately, not the total norm. In the step-150 checkpoint manifest (`opt_state`), the groups hold these parameters: AdamH holds `output_proj`; Adam holds `token_embed`, `embed_norm`, `final_norm`, the routers, router bias, attention gates and the expert MLPs (`expert_mlp` w_gate and w_up stored as `[26, 256, 2560, 1280]`, w_down as `[26, 256, 1280, 2560]`); MuonH holds the other matrices, the gated norms and the stacked `rms_attn`/`rms_mlp` weights (stored as `[26, 2560]`). So the binding count uses the group norms. In the clip run, the MuonH group was above 1.0 on 8 updates, AdamH on 13 and Adam on none. Nearly all of it is the first 13 updates plus 4 later spikes.
- **Where the numbers come from:** W&B logs `grad/norm/<parameter>` before the optimizer, so these are pre-clip norms. Each group norm is rebuilt from the 27 logged per-parameter norms, using the optimizer's own grouping rule. Their sum of squares matches the logged `grad/norm/total` within 1% on every update.
- **The loss curves are not equal step by step.** They differ on every one of the 150 updates, starting at update 1 by 0.00004 (0.79061 vs 0.79058).
  - Update 1's loss is computed before any update, so clipping cannot explain that first gap. It comes from the different cluster and executable, not from clipping.
  - Clipping can act from update 2 on. Mean absolute gap over updates 2-150 is 0.00034, and 12 updates differ by more than 0.001. The largest gap is 0.0044, at update 79, where the no-clip run had its one large spike (MuonH group norm 9.00 and Adam group norm 1.50, against 0.23 and 0.06 in the clip run).
- **Reading, not a conclusion:**
  - Clipping bound on 14 of 150 updates, mostly in the first 13. Train loss ended the same to the third decimal.
  - On held-out sets, no clip is 0.003-0.005 lower on all, SFT and SFT macro than clip 1.0. Replay pretrain, Nemotron and agenttrove are within 0.001.
  - Identity-data is 0.047 lower without clipping. It rests on 8 held-out packed sequences, and every arm drew 3 identity sequences in training (method caveat: https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/11783#issuecomment-7056481299).
    - **Correction (21 Nov):** updated the identity draw count from `1` → `3` packed sequences in 150 updates; the earlier realized-mix tool listed data sources in sorted order, whereas training uses config order (`MixtureDataset` insertion order).
  - These are single runs. The clip pair also crosses clusters, so a 0.003 gap is not separable from cross-cluster numeric noise without a repeat.
- **Weights:**
  - control (LR 2e-5): `s3://marin-us-east-02a/tmp/ttl=30d/long-loop-436/base-start-20261118/control-eager/checkpoints/step-150` ([Filer](https://filer.marina.oa.dev/#s3%3A%2F%2Fmarin-us-east-02a%2Ftmp%2Fttl%3D30d%2Flong-loop-436%2Fbase-start-20261118%2Fcontrol-eager%2Fcheckpoints%2Fstep-150))

comments.author: XiaoyuanWang111
comments.body:
🤖 The public checkpoints test the hypothesis in the BF16-vs-FP32 comment and settle the unverified detail. Exp1 is `open-athena/Snowball-LongLoop-Round1-2026.11.12.7` (`475ba62d`), Exp2 is `open-athena/Snowball-LongLoop-Round2-2026.11.14.13` (`6546ba2d`) and Exp3 is `open-athena/Snowball-LongLoop-Round3-2026.11.17.55` (`8e787c61`). Each is compared with the base `open-athena/snowball-67b-a2b-base-262k-qk175-skew8` (`3bbf729f`), so the numbers include each round's RL updates.

**BF16 storage rounded away most of Exp1's Muon-H updates.** After 746 SFT updates at 5e-5, 77% of Exp1's attention values are bit-identical to the base and 17% differ by one BF16 step. The Muon-H matrices moved 0.20%, and most of that is the hyperball re-projection rounding the stored values, `bf16(bf16(x / n) * n)`, which #11755 removes: measured from the re-projected base, they moved 0.125%. With FP32 storage, Exp2 and Exp3 moved the attention matrices 3.26% and 1.02%.

**The unverified detail.** On Exp1's stacked `(L, D)` RMSNorm scales, the Muon-H step left nothing that BF16 storage kept. 13.1% of the 133,120 scale values changed, 95.4% of the changed values equal what the re-projection alone gives from the base, and 99.5% of the values that the re-projection flips are flipped. The re-projection takes `n` over the whole leaf: `input_layernorm` (26 × 2560) needs `n = 336`, and its float64 norm is 335.03. What the orthogonalized step itself did stayed below one BF16 step, so the weights cannot show it.

**Where each round's update landed** (displacement `|round − base| / |base|` per class, then the share of values that changed):

| tensor class | Exp1 (BF16 storage) | Exp2 (FP32, Adam on all) | Exp3 (FP32, Hero-EP routing) |
|---|---|---|---|
| routed expert banks | 9.79%, 85.4% (Adam) | 3.60%, 94.9% | 0.79%, 76.7% (Muon-H) |
| attention q, k, v, o | 0.20%, 22.8% (Muon-H) | 3.26%, 93.9% | 1.02%, 82.1% |
| shared expert | 0.20%, 24.1% (Muon-H) | 3.40%, 94.7% | 1.06%, 83.7% |
| GatedNorm projections | 0.22%, 26.5% (Muon-H) | 3.24%, 95.0% | 1.10%, 83.3% |
| `lm_head` | 1.15%, 9.3% (AdamH) | 3.97%, 96.4% | 1.32%, 78.4% |

Exp1 is the only round whose always-active matrices barely moved, while its Adam fall-through moved the expert banks 9.79%. So Arm 1 (FP32 storage) and Arm 2 (expert banks on Muon-H) also change where the update lands, and a per-class displacement count of each arm's checkpoint against the base shows that before any eval. Method: #11687 and #11639.

comments.author: XiaoyuanWang111
comments.body: 🤖 Arm C's drop matches what BF16 storage did to Exp1 (my comment above): a stored BF16 weight changes only when a step exceeds half a BF16 step, so smaller steps are lost at every update and never accumulate. On Exp1, after 746 updates at 5e-5, 77% of the attention values were still bit-identical to the base and the Muon-H matrices moved 0.20%, mostly the re-projection's rounding, while the Adam-updated expert banks moved 9.79%. If arm C's optimizer layout matches Exp1's, its attention, shared-expert and GatedNorm matrices have barely moved by step 150, so arm C differs from the control in which parameters trained, not only in storage precision. The finish reasons point the same way: 180 tool-call finishes against 908. Counting, per parameter class, the values in arm C's export that are bit-identical to its start checkpoint would confirm or rule this out in a few CPU minutes, without another eval.

🤖

## Optimizer: arm E r2 (MoE expert banks on Adam) vs the 19 Nov control at seed 0 and seed 2, held-out loss (one hour, step 150)

All runs use the 19 Nov / 6164 data and model, FP32 stored weights, 20.47% replay and 150 updates. The score is all-token held-out loss, and the scorer loads FP32 params. Each run was scored in the cluster it was trained in, with the same eval config. Each cell is one training run.

**No control matches arm E r2 in both seed and cluster.** Arm E r2 was trained with seed 0 on cw-rno2a. The seed-0 control has the same seed but was trained on cw-us-east-02a. The seed-2 control was trained on the same cluster (cw-rno2a) with another seed. The two controls differ from each other by +0.0121 on held-out SFT (seed 2 − seed 0); read arm E r2's gaps against that spread.

## Optimizer groups

Read from the optimizer state saved in each step-150 checkpoint.

- **Control (both seeds):**
  - Muon-H on 18 arrays: attention w_q, w_k, w_v, w_o; MoE expert banks w_gate, w_up, w_down; shared MLP w_gate, w_up, w_down; GatedNorm w_down and w_up in the embed, attention, MLP and final GatedNorms.
  - AdamH on output_proj.
  - Adam on 8 arrays: token embedding, embed norm, attention RMS norm, attention gate, MLP RMS norm, router, router bias, final norm.
- **Arm E r2:** the three MoE expert banks (w_gate, w_up, w_down) move from Muon-H to Adam. The setting is `optimizer.muonh_param_ndims = [2, 3]`, so the 4-D bank arrays leave Muon-H.
  - Muon-H on the other 15 arrays.
  - AdamH on output_proj.
  - Adam on 11 arrays: the same 8 plus the three expert banks. The banks use the control's Adam settings: Adam learning rate 2e-5, beta1 0.9062, beta2 0.95, epsilon 3.83e-15.
- **All runs:** the global gradient norm is clipped to 1.0. Learning rates, schedule and weight decay are equal.

## Other config differences

Bookkeeping below means run ids, tracker names, and log, checkpoint, timing and sharding-dump paths.

- **Arm E r2 vs the seed-2 control:** the seed (0 vs 2), `muonh_param_ndims` and bookkeeping. The code differs only in the commit that adds `muonh_param_ndims`; its default keeps the control routing.
- **Arm E r2 vs the seed-0 control:**
  - `muonh_param_ndims`;
  - the training cluster and its bucket paths (cw-rno2a vs cw-us-east-02a);
  - a post-rebind host barrier with an 1800 s timeout, which the seed-0 control did not have;
  - bookkeeping.

## Held-out loss (lower is better)

| replay pretrain (mean of the 4 sets) | 0.8578 | 0.8538 | 0.8536 | +0.0041 | +0.0042 | −0.0001 | 0.8804 |
| pretrain c13q3 | 0.3504 | 0.3582 | 0.3571 | −0.0078 | −0.0066 | −0.0011 | 0.3597 |

## Reading

- **SFT sources:** arm E r2 is lower than both controls on all 10 SFT sources.
  - Against seed 0, the largest gaps are identity-data (−0.6762), finance (−0.2437) and interactive agent (−0.1992).
  - Against seed 2, they are identity-data (−0.8268), finance (−0.2385) and interactive agent (−0.1833).
  - The smallest gap is code_zh (−0.0097 against seed 0, −0.0099 against seed 2).
- **Without identity-data,** arm E r2's SFT source macro is 0.0745 below seed 0 and 0.0727 below seed 2. The two controls differ by 0.0017 on this measure.
- **Replay pretrain:**
  - Arm E r2 is 0.0041 above seed 0, 0.0042 above seed 2, and 0.0018 above the step-0 base (0.8561). Both controls are below the base.

  - Arm E r2 read the same rows as the seed-0 control (same seed, data block and mixture weights), so both drew 3 identity sequences in 150 updates, at the same positions.
  - The seed-2 control drew 2. Arm D-r2 has the same seed and data block as the seed-0 control.

comments.author: XiaoyuanWang111
comments.body:
🤖 Arm F splits the two ways Adam differs from Muon-H on the banks. It keeps the per-coordinate normalization and drops the momentum, and it lands with arm E: Micro210 49.57% against 50.19%, +22.81 and +23.42 pp over the matched control. Its SFT loss sits between the two (0.536 against 0.488 for arm E and 0.648 for the control), so momentum may add a little, but most of the gain comes without it. That leaves the size of the step.

At the same rate the two kinds of rule take very different steps on a bank. Adam and the RMS rule scale each coordinate by the running RMS of its own gradient, so one update moves each coordinate by up to about the rate, 2e-5. Muon-H's hyperball update moves a bank by the rate times its Frobenius norm, which is 2e-5 × RMS(W) per coordinate. In the public long-loop base (`open-athena/snowball-67b-a2b-base-262k-qk175-skew8`) the routed experts have RMS(W) = 0.00975, so if the banks these arms start from are of that scale, the Muon-H step is about 100 times smaller per coordinate, and 150 updates move a bank by at most 0.3% of its norm. Exp1's Adam-updated banks show the full-size steps: on values below 2^-9, where BF16 rounding does not interfere, their RMS change is 1.34e-3, and 746 full-size steps of 5e-5 with uncorrelated signs give 5e-5 × √746 = 1.37e-3.

If the step size is the cause, Muon-H banks with a bank-only rate near 2e-5 / 0.00975 ≈ 2e-3 should close most of the gap. One more one-hour arm like E and F would test it, and would show whether the banks need a different rule or only a larger step.

🤖

## Held-out loss: arm E r2 (MoE expert banks on Adam) vs the 20.47% control, eight hours (steps 250 and 500)

Both runs use the 19 Nov / 6164 data and model, FP32 stored weights, 20.47% replay and 500 updates, with trainer seed 0. Both were trained and scored on cw-rno2a with the 1,800 s post-rebind barrier. Arm E r2 puts the 4-D expert banks on Adam; the control keeps Muon-H on every matrix. Each column is one training run, scored at its permanent step-250 and step-500 saves.

## What differs between the two runs

- **Matched pair:** same seed, cluster and barrier.
- **Config:** the consumed training configs (18,424 leaves) differ in one setting after run names, ids and output paths: the bank routing (`optimizer.muonh_param_ndims` is `[2, 3]` for arm E r2 and left at its default, which includes the 4-D banks, for the control).
- **Code:** both runs use the same code commit, which includes the temporary-checkpoint changes from PR 11719. Unlike the one-hour pairs, this pair has no other code difference (no logging or state-snapshot change between the two), so it is an optimizer-routing-only comparison.
- **Against the one-hour arm E r2 run:** the eight-hour arm E r2 config differs only in the number of updates (150 → 500), the checkpoint interval (150 → 250), the task timeout and run names and paths.

🤖

## Mochi Bank-RMS probes: the line stops

We ran short probes of the RMSProp-style expert-bank rule on Mochi. The rule keeps a second moment only and has no momentum. Each probe restored Mochi's step-400407 SFT checkpoint and ran 20 updates (400407..400426). The reference twin is the production Muon-H run from the same checkpoint. All runs share update 400407, so the means below cover the 19 updates after it (400408..400426).

The rule was written before the last probe ran: mean loss within 1.05x of the twin, and no grad norm above 5.

| probe | mean loss, 400408..400426 | ratio to twin | grad norm | written rule |
|---|---:|---:|---|---|
| Twin (Muon-H, production) | 0.483053 | 1.000 | 0.35 to 1.26 | reference |
| Control v2 (Muon-H banks, probe commit) | 0.483036 | 1.000 | max 0.737 | pass |
| Bank-RMS, cold start (bank state zero, full LR) | 0.828535 | 1.715 | 218.67 at 400413 | fail |
| Bank-RMS, warm second moment (20 warm-up passes, full LR) | 0.629574 | 1.303 | 136.21 at 400415 | fail |
| Bank-RMS, warm second moment, 0.25x bank LR | 0.521396 | 1.079 | 10.44 at 400409, 5.88 at 400413 | fail |

## What the probes show

- **Code ruled out.** Control v2 ran the same commit as the cold probe, with Muon-H on the banks. It matched the twin (1.000x, no spike at 400413). So the gap in the cold probe comes from the bank rule with fresh state, not from the newer code base.
- **The cold start is not the main cause.** Warming the second moment removed the 400413 spike (loss 0.667 against 3.711 cold). Most of the gap stayed: 1.29x the twin without 400413, against 1.38x cold.
- **Warm start plus a 0.25x bank LR is still 1.079x the twin and unstable.** All 19 updates are above the twin (1.014x to 1.261x per update). The grad norm passes 5 twice.
- **Snowball is not a like-for-like guide.** In Snowball, the bank arms were ahead of their own controls from update 1 (loss ratio 0.984 at update 1 in all three pairs). Their mean loss ratios over updates 2..20 were 0.913, 0.954 and 0.922; the one with the same RMSProp-style rule was 0.954. But each Snowball pair is two cold starts from the pre-train base with every optimizer slot fresh. Mochi sets a fresh bank state against a warm Muon-H twin mid-schedule.

## Decision

- Under the written rule, the Mochi Bank-RMS line stops here. There will be no 8-hour Mochi Bank-RMS run.
- A like-for-like test would need a fresh-optimizer start from Mochi's pre-train base.

issues.author: penfever
issues.body:
TL;DR: Model merging is a promising direction for Marin: different Grug/Snowball checkpoints have complementary strengths, but we do not yet have a reliable way to combine them while preserving the base model's other capabilities. Cheap weight-space operations could make this orders of magnitude less expensive than on-policy distillation (OPD). We would benefit from expert input on how to make that tradeoff work for our mixture-of-experts (MoE) models.

The policy evaluation tracker illustrates the problem (percentages; higher is better):

| Checkpoint | MATH500 | GPQA-Diamond | HumanEval+ | NUPA | BFCL-Parity/Pi |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| [Grug Antidoom Step12](https://huggingface.co/open-athena/Grug-67B-A2B-Antidoom-RLVR1-Step12-2026.10.02) | 95.00 | 67.30 | 72.60 | 0.10 | 5.70 |
| [Snowball Mixed-RLVR Step92](https://huggingface.co/open-athena/Snowball-67B-A2B-10T-Mixed-RLVR-Sync-Step92) | 89.60 | 42.90 | 68.90 | 40.60 | 16.30 |
| [Grug Reference-KL Step20](https://huggingface.co/open-athena/Grug-67B-A2B-Antidoom-RLVR1-Reference-KL-Step20-2026.10.04) | 92.60 | 63.00 | 86.60 | 0.30 | 43.90 |

Source: [policy-tracker snapshot](https://huggingface.co/datasets/open-athena/Snowball-67B-A2B-Model-Merging-Artifacts-2026.10.09/blob/c4fb17eb44005e01cbb3d5b38c672a2ffa473880/artifacts/inputs/TRACKER.md). These are policy NUPA scores; the merge study instead optimized NUPA200, a 200-task subset of the policy’s 5,000-task panel. BFCL-Parity/Pi is the policy's tool-use evaluation with the Pi agent. No checkpoint in this comparison achieves the best score in every column.

Our [initial study](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/9975) shows both the appeal and the unresolved problem. Static merge construction typically required roughly 1e11–1e12 estimated arithmetic FLOPs per checkpoint, often without GPUs. This supports the prospect of a large compute advantage over OPD, which requires rollout generation and training; we have not run a matched OPD cost comparison. Evaluation and any calibration or expert-selection work add costs beyond static construction.

The best merge scored 36.50% on NUPA200 and 48.78% on BFCL-Parity, versus historical specialist references of 38.00% and 43.90%, respectively. But its recipe copied only 0.76% of all parameter values unchanged from the intended Base (Step12). On non-target benchmarks, it scored 89.80% MATH500 and 52.19% GPQA-Diamond, versus Base’s historical policy scores of 95.00% and 67.30%; these were not matched reruns. That study did not establish capability-preserving transfer into Base.

We would welcome advice from people with model-merging experience, especially on transferring specialist behavior into an existing MoE checkpoint with limited weight changes, handling expert/router compatibility and the tokenizer differences observed in #9975, and choosing retention evaluations that expose damage outside the target benchmarks.

Done when: expert feedback informs a concrete follow-up design with a fixed Base, explicit limits on weight changes, and pre-agreed target and non-target evaluation criteria.

comments.author: loom-oa-dev[bot]
comments.body:
🤖
# Research

The best merge in [#9975](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/9975) scored 36.50% NUPA200 and 48.78% BFCL-Parity, but copied only 0.76% of Base weights unchanged; its lower MATH500 and GPQA-Diamond scores are historical comparisons, not matched retention tests. Changing the loading and tokenizer bundle alone moved BFCL-Parity from 0.81% to 17.07% with NUPA weights fixed, so the earlier search cannot isolate weight transfer. [PR #9974](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/9974) already supplies merging tools, but does not enforce the later 25% change budget; the [earlier follow-up outline](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/9975#issuecomment-6074700342) belongs here as a Base-anchored study.

**Relevant code**
- [`merge.py`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/1c2b6517e1449f37e54d183255d5a453cf4d4ee8/experiments/weight_merging/merge.py#L19-L42) — checkpoint export entry point.

# Proposed Fix

1. Pin Step12 as Base and pin both donor revisions. Run matched Base and donor evaluations with identical prompts and decoding; hold Base configuration, tokenizer, chat template, and generation settings fixed for merge candidates, with separate tokenizer and special-token-row controls.
2. After #9974 lands, verify tensor and expert-row alignment, then add an export audit that counts changed scalar positions against Base at stored dtype, globally and by component. Reject any candidate above a 25% change budget; report router, shared-expert, routed-expert, attention, and embedding changes separately.
3. Predeclare 5%, 10%, and 25% budgets and compare Base-anchored activation-ranked NUPA/BFCL expert transfers with matched random-expert and no-transfer controls. Record routing changes and collect fresh activation data because the archive lacks the transcripts needed for exact replay.
4. Freeze NUPA200 and BFCL-Parity as target tests, and MATH500, GPQA-Diamond, and HumanEval+ as retention sentinels; run the full policy cohort on finalists. Agree numeric target gains and maximum retention losses after matched baseline repeats but before candidate scoring, then publish recipes, checkpoint revisions, changed-weight counts, all scores, negative results, and construction/calibration/evaluation costs. Advance a candidate only if both targets improve and every retention floor passes.

Expert feedback requested: Is Base-router compatibility adequately tested by matched activation and routing checks, or should expert alignment use a different control? Are the proposed tokenizer controls and retention sentinels sufficient to detect damage outside NUPA and BFCL?

comments.author: craffel
comments.body:
Hi, I can comment a bit on this (also tagging @marcociccone who has been doing a lot of work along these lines).

Anecdotally it seems that merging may work better* than OPD in the MOPD setup when merging RL-trained checkpoints:
- [This paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.12566) which seems to have invented MOPD without credit (?) includes merging as a baseline, where it compares favorably.
- The ["MOPD paper"](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.30406) includes task arithmetic (a weak merging baseline) where it performs roughly on par with OPD
- The [Open-MOPD paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.19098) also has some merging results and it works reasonably well.
- [This very recent paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.04272) also has some promising results with merging in the MOPD setting.
- The fact that merging can work well in the RL setting is explored in [this paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.22039).

The trouble is that there is some conflicting evidence, which I think stems from the following:
- We generally do not have a precise characterization of how well merging will work in a particular setting.
- Most work that evaluates merging takes the simplest possible method off the shelf (generally task arithmetic). This can work ok (anecdotally especially for larger models, see [here](https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.03617)) but there has been a ton of work on more sophisticated merging methods that have been pretty conclusively demonstrated to work better. The additional trouble, though, is that there are details that people often get wrong, for example how to merge the embedding/unembedding matrices, or other nuisance details (see e.g. the discussion of incorrect implementations of RegMean in [our recent work](https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.01329)).
- Underlying merging is the choice of mixing coefficients for the constituent models, which is rarely explored but turns out to be important in practice.
- To get to the asterisk above, there often is only a cursory notion of what "better" means; often it is found e.g. that merging works better than MT/OPD on some tasks and worse on others, but this seems to largely be a consequence of the implicit mixing weights used by a merging method where no mixing weight tuning is done.

As mentioned above @marcociccone is finishing up a project investigating this much more thoroughly; the end product is a method for tuning merging coefficients and strong results using strong merging methods. It's a bit hard to claim "pareto-optimality" in terms of the merged model dominating the MT/OPD model for *every* task, but merging at the very least seems to be on par and also has the huge advantage of being much cheaper to use (and in particular much cheaper to try out new mixing coefficients to balance capabilities to your preferred profile).

HTH.

comments.body:
🤖 A data point on the transfer losses in #9920 and #9984: both experts were trained on targets that never open a reasoning block, and every distilled arm, and the half-strength merge, carries that shape to prompts outside CRUXEval. That fits the off-target losses better than skill interference does.

**Expert data.** The SFT rows of expert E ([`task133-20261007-prepared-v2`](https://huggingface.co/datasets/open-athena/Snowball-67B-A2B-CruxEval-Transfer-Artifacts-2026.10/tree/98c153c05ddd02068c5415144696e01e9a61c0a2/teacher-traces/cruxeval-test-exposed/task133-20261007-prepared-v2)) and expert E2 ([`task162-e2-prepared-20261009-v1`](https://huggingface.co/datasets/open-athena/Snowball-67B-A2B-Two-Expert-Transfer-Artifacts-2026.10/tree/7a96dade2635b0bd76a1a67cb5381fad2d6b2be8/teacher-traces/mopd2/task162-e2-prepared-20261009-v1)) put the reasoning inline: `reasoning\n<|end_think|>\n\nanswer`. The `chat_template.jinja` shipped with them renders assistant `content` verbatim and ends the generation prompt at the assistant header, so `<|start_think|>` is in neither the prompt nor the target. `MARIN_CHAT_TEMPLATE` renders reasoning as `<|start_think|>…<|end_think|>` ([`chat_template.py` L109](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/f79686b2185c57d2db32569d9c27f2bcebd04e76/lib/marin/src/marin/datakit/chat_template.py#L109)).

| SFT rows | rows | with `<\|start_think\|>` | with one `<\|end_think\|>` |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| expert E | 1,454 | 0 | 1,454 |
| expert E2 | 1,359 | 0 | 1,359 |

The counts are the same in `train.jsonl` and in the token ids of `train-prebuilt.jsonl.gz`.

**What E learned.** Of E's 12,800 k=8 samples (`task145-e-k8-20261008`), 98 have one well-formed block; 11,133 have no reasoning before the first `<|end_think|>`, 4,747 repeat the opener and 1,679 reopen after closing. The plain and RS-SFT sets are drawn from these samples: none of the 1,503 RS-SFT targets starts with `<|start_think|>`, and 711 contain two or more. For comparison, #10400 finds two or more thinking segments in 1.9% to 9.1% of the thinking messages of Marin's general checkpoints.

**What the arms carry.** Teacher-forced next-token probabilities on 48 prompts (12 each from CRUXEval, MMLU-Pro, GSM8K and IFEval) for the checkpoints #9920 and #9984 pin, averaged over the 36 prompts that are not CRUXEval:

| | B | E | RS-SFT 282 | OPD 75 | plain SFT 399 | mixed RS 727 | MOPD 100 | merge TA0.5 |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| `/think`, after `<\|start_think\|>\n`: next token closes or reopens | 0.0016 | 0.156 | 0.220 | 0.216 | 0.298 | 0.376 | 0.829 | 0.152 |
| `/nothink`: first token is `<\|start_think\|>` | 0.0000 | 0.051 | 0.288 | 0.041 | 0.373 | 0.274 | 0.420 | 0.115 |

On the CRUXEval prompts under `/nothink` the opener probability is 0.95 for RS-SFT and 0.78 for OPD (B 0.00), in line with the think blocks the #9920 and #9984 panels counted in thinking-off CRUXEval replies (28 and 18 of 30; v0.1 0). B itself writes a second opener after `<|start_think|>\n` on the CRUXEval prompt format (0.91, against 0.0015 on the other prompts), so part of the CRUXEval gap that E closes is format.

**Reading.** The off-target losses sit on format-strict benchmarks (BFCL-Parity, NUPA with 62.8% to 71.9% valid format, thinking-off FinanceBench, length-capped TriviaQA), while knowledge and reasoning benchmarks hold. Every expert row has the shape #11706 describes: reasoning without the opener, then `<|end_think|>`. The probe shows that the arms carry it, not that it causes the losses, and how far an arm shifts does not rank its BFCL loss. A direct test: re-score B on the affected benchmarks with the current panel code (B's panel row is from older code), then compare RS282 with RS-SFT on the same samples rewritten into one well-formed block each, and with an expert rebuilt from the GLM traces rendered with the opener. If the format is fixed and the losses stay, the format is not the cause.

comments.author: marcociccone
comments.body:
Hey @penfever, sorry for the late reply on this thread! I’m currently wrapping up the project @craffel mentioned.

What we’ve noticed is that, in the end, most merging methods are fairly equivalent if you have enough compute for evaluation to tune the merging weights and scaling coefficients of the task vectors. That’s really what gives you the edge.

Spectral methods work great for merging, though they can be brittle, so you have to be careful about which matrices you apply them to, as well as the SVD precision. Generally, a combination of averaging and SVD-based methods works best.

Happy to chat more about this and share our preprint!

comments.author: XiaoyuanWang111
comments.body:
🤖 @marcociccone, measurements on Marin's public checkpoints bear on both of your points. On coefficients: the coefficient a merge applies is not always the one it is given. `dare-ties-02` stores a fivefold extrapolation where its recipe says 0.5 (point 2), and a rounding rule that reproduces #10700's numbers puts the realized coefficients of that BF16 ladder at 0.19 for α = 0.5 and 0.65 for α = 1 (point 3). On which matrices: on this MoE the choice matters for plain task arithmetic too. The full-strength merge of #9984 leaves 30 of 48 GSM8K replies without a stop token, and holding its 78 attention GatedNorm and attention-gate tensors (0.027% of the weights) at the anchor's values removes that (point 4). I'd be glad to read the preprint.

Below are three measurements on the public checkpoints that bear on the design of the follow-up study, and what a causal test of the full-strength merge of #9984 adds (point 4). I read tensors over HTTP range requests, with no GPU; scripts, tables and the test for points 2 to 4 are in [grug-weight-atlas](https://github.com/XiaoyuanWang111/grug-weight-atlas/tree/6ed4484582c36281319c8b30763c11fee083722d/). Point 1 comes from a later read of 13 checkpoints; I can post its script and distance matrices. The test itself is reported on #9984.

**1. The NUPA donor's delta against Base is the distance between two training lines.** #9975 left the ancestry open ("NUPA's exact common ancestor with Base remains unestablished"). The family tree on main puts Step92 under the skew4 long-context extension and Datakit SFT 09.11, and Step12 under the skew8 extension and Datakit SFT 09.21. The two extensions are sibling runs of 1,000 updates from the final cooldown, so the two lines share only the pretraining run. Distances in percent of the skew4 extension's weight norm (all 26 layers; 32 of 256 routed experts per layer, attention and the shared expert in full):

| pair | routed experts | attention q, k, v, o | shared expert |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| skew8 extension, skew4 extension | 2.77 | 2.92 | 2.59 |
| skew8 extension, Step12 | 1.22 | 1.52 | 1.54 |
| skew4 extension, Step92 | 1.59 | 1.90 | 1.88 |
| Step12, Step92 | 3.36 | 3.64 | 3.41 |
| Step12, Datakit SFT 09.21 | 0.06 | 0.16 | 0.16 |
| Step92, RLVR2-Sync-Step116 | 0.22 | 0.25 | 0.24 |
| Step92, RLVR-Async-Step92 | 0.60 | 0.65 | 0.66 |

The two lines were already 2.6% to 2.9% apart after their long-context extensions, and each line's post-training added 1.2% to 1.9%. The two RLVR arms that started from Datakit SFT 09.11 are 0.60% apart. They moved equally far (seen from the skew4 extension, their parent projects onto the midpoint between them), and the updates each made after step 92 are orthogonal (cosine 0.000). If their first 92 steps were orthogonal too, each arm is 0.42% from Datakit SFT 09.11. On that reading the donor's own RLVR training is about 1.6% of the energy of `Step92 − Step12`, and the rest was there before any RLVR step.

This fits what the campaigns saw. In Campaign 1, NUPA came across with the feed-forward weights of layers 13 to 25 of the Step92 line (26.0 in a Step20 body) and not with 32 NUPA-selected experts per layer (1.0). None of Campaign 2's 48 Base-anchored merges scored above 10 on NUPA200, while the BFCL delta, whose donor descends from Base, transferred inside a 25% support.

The donor's own task vector is `Step92 − Datakit-SFT-262K-2026.09.11`. That checkpoint is not public, so I could not measure it. `merge_checkpoint` can apply it to Base as it is: task arithmetic anchored at SFT 09.11 with donors Step92 and Step12 at 1.0 gives `Step12 + Step92 − SFT 09.11` (the output takes the anchor's metadata files, so Base's have to be copied over it). Whether an RL delta still works on weights 3.4% away from where it was learned is open; that merge would answer it.

**2. What `dare-ties-02` stores.** I read 18 supported expert rows in full (layers 0, 12 and 25, the three projections, two rows each) and 9 rows outside the support. All 13,953,740 changed values are bit-exact `Base + 5 × (donor − Base)`: 77.0% with Step92's delta, 20.6% with Step20's and 2.4% with the mean of the two. The rows outside the support equal Base. This is what the two steps described in #9975 give when combined: DARE divides the kept 20% by the density, and the TIES step divides by the coefficient mass, which cancels the 0.5 wherever one donor survives. So the recipe's 0.5 coefficients do not scale the update, and every changed value is a fivefold extrapolation.

The supported rows sit 3.6% to 10.5% from Base with 22% to 25% of their values changed; Step92's own rows are 1.6% to 4.7% away. So the changed-scalar count does not bound how far a merge moves the weights it touches. And about three quarters of this merge's 6.04% went to the cross-line delta of point 1, which scored NUPA200 0.00.

Those values are still in the released models. In six of these rows, Marin-Snowball-67B-A2B-v0.1 keeps 71% to 97% of the Step92-delta values bit-identical to the merge, and its distance from the merge on those positions is under 0.6% of the written delta; for v0.1.1 it is 0.4% to 2.0%.

**3. What a BF16 checkpoint keeps of an update (extends #10700).** Each public child of Step92 fits `child = round_to_BF16(parent + u)`, with u drawn from N(0, σ²) and one σ per checkpoint, the same for small and large weights. A stored value changes only when |u| exceeds half a BF16 step at that weight. On `model.layers.12.self_attn.q_proj.weight` this reproduces the share of changed values in each of 14 binades within 0.6 points for six children (σ from 7.6e-6 to 4.2e-5). Fitting σ to the one number "69.6% erased at α = 1" of #10700 predicts its α = 0.5 point: 16.13% of entries changed (reported 16.15%) and 83.53% erased (reported 83.51%). Under this rule the ladder's realized coefficients are 0.19 at α = 0.5, 0.40 at 0.75, 0.52 at 0.875 and 0.65 at 1.

For a budgeted study this means the changed-scalar count of a whole-model fine-tune measures its step size, not how local it is: the eight fine-tunes of Step92 change 15% to 61% of stored scalars, though each changes values in every attention, expert, router-weight and GatedNorm tensor.

**4. Where the full-strength merge of #9984 breaks, and what full strength gains.** In a pre-registered CPU test, the rebuilt full-strength merge left 30 of 48 GSM8K replies without a stop token within 4,096 tokens, and the same merge with its 78 attention GatedNorm and attention-gate tensors held at the values of its anchor, Step92, left none; these tensors are 0.027% of the weights and sit in the plain-Adam group of `GrugMoeAdamHConfig.create_mask`. So these 78 tensors are where this full-strength merge breaks, and holding them at the anchor's values removes the failure in this case. That merge then scores like Merge-TA0.5 on #9984's targets (CRUXEval input and output and MMLU-Pro, 270 prompts each): the composite difference is +0.011, with a 95% interval from -0.025 to +0.047. On these targets a = b = 1.0 gained nothing measurable over 0.5. The test covers one expert pair.

Limits: point 1 reads 32 of 256 routed experts per layer; point 2 rests on 18 expert rows in three layers; the 1.6% in point 1 assumes the two RLVR arms were orthogonal before step 92 as they are after it.

issues.body:
## TL;DR

Add a pinned generative OpenAI MRCR task to Marin's served evaluation path and run a bounded smoke against the registered Snowball 67B S3 export. Issue #8701 measured teacher-forced response likelihood; this follow-up requires the model to generate the requested prior response and its nonce.

## Description

Marin's pinned Evalchemy runtime has no working MRCR task. The new task should use OpenAI MRCR revision `f4c69fae7cf81f7ca26b9fee34b392a50f6b8a1d`, preserve the dataset's message order, render explicit `User:` and `Assistant:` roles for the base model, and call the completions endpoint. The scorer must return zero when the response omits the nonce, then remove the nonce from both response and gold before applying `difflib.SequenceMatcher`.

The first run should use the existing `snowball` export at `s3://marin-us-east-02a/marin/exports/grug/june-67b-a2b/step-42150/hf-bf16-vllm/d819cbc63780bd86/`. It should select one example from each MRCR length-bin and needle-count cell that fits the server's advertised context, use deterministic greedy decoding, and preserve raw prompts, generations, per-sample scores, prefix-hit rate, and cell coverage.

## Hypothesis or Goal

The shared evaluation launcher can serve Snowball on CoreWeave, execute canonical MRCR generation through Evalchemy, and write scored sample artifacts without a new checkpoint export. A successful smoke establishes the evaluator and serving path needed for the step-141000/156000/157000 checkpoints in #8701.

## Status

Implemented in #8706. Smoke run `20260826-180537-snowball-mrcr-smoke-40df` succeeded across all 12 context-fitting cells with zero Iris failures or preemptions.

## Links

* Paired likelihood experiment: #8701
* Implementation: #8706
* Dataset: https://huggingface.co/datasets/openai/mrcr/tree/f4c69fae7cf81f7ca26b9fee34b392a50f6b8a1d
* Run evidence: https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/8702#issuecomment-5430184744
* Durable results: `s3://marin-us-east-02a/marin/evals/20260826-180537-snowball-mrcr-smoke-40df/results`
* Logbook: none
* W&B Report: none

## Decision Log

* Use the existing Snowball S3 export before exporting the #8701 checkpoints.
* Keep the task definition in Marin and load it through Evalchemy's local task path.
* Use completion-style prompts with explicit role labels because the evaluated checkpoint is a base model.
* Use greedy decoding for reproducible checkpoint comparisons; do not compare the score directly with OpenAI's sampled API results.

## Conclusion

The Snowball export serves real MRCR through the shared CoreWeave path and writes complete scored artifacts, so no additional export work is needed for this checkpoint. Model quality is low: aggregate MRCR accuracy was `0.004714223641098665`, and only 2 of 12 generations passed the exact nonce-prefix gate. The evaluator is ready to use after exporting the step-141000/156000/157000 checkpoints from #8701.

🤖 **Analysis — not opening a PR (multi-repo experiment + cluster smoke).**

This is an experiment that spans the pinned Evalchemy fork and a live CoreWeave serve→eval run, not a self-contained code fix. The generative MRCR task (dataset load at the pinned revision, `User:`/`Assistant:` rendering, completions endpoint, nonce-gated `SequenceMatcher` scorer) has to land in the fork; Marin only pins its commit and selects the task. The smoke also needs an 8×H100 CoreWeave node to serve Snowball, which I can't run here. Handing back root cause and a proposed approach for review.

The MRCR task does not exist in Marin — the task body lives in the external Evalchemy fork, which Marin pins by commit. Marin's served path already builds a per-task run config (`generation`, `completion_only`, `max_length`) and hands the served OpenAI URL to the Evalchemy child; task selection is a small config yaml. - [`external_dependencies.py` L55-62](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/8e27d964c1e3852f755036e74314a230a9920381/lib/marin/src/marin/external_dependencies.py#L55-L62) — `EVALCHEMY` fork pin; the MRCR task and scorer land here, then re-pin `commit`.
- [`evalchemy/runner.py` L141-181](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/8e27d964c1e3852f755036e74314a230a9920381/lib/marin/src/marin/evaluation/evalchemy/runner.py#L141-L181) — per-task `dir`/`generation`/`completion_only`/`max_length` and `extra_gen_kwargs` passed to the served run.
- [`models.py` L119-123](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/8e27d964c1e3852f755036e74314a230a9920381/experiments/evaluation/models.py#L119-L123) — `snowball` export already registered with `CONCAT_CHAT_TEMPLATE` and EP/DP on 8×H100.
- [`configs/evalchemy/gsm8k-smoke.yaml`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/8e27d964c1e3852f755036e74314a230a9920381/experiments/evaluation/configs/evalchemy/gsm8k-smoke.yaml) — config-yaml pattern (`tasks` + `task_options` + `limit`) a new `mrcr.yaml` mirrors.

**Proposed approach**

1. In the Evalchemy fork, add the generative MRCR task at revision `f4c69fae7cf81f7ca26b9fee34b392a50f6b8a1d`: preserve message order, render explicit `User:`/`Assistant:` roles, call completions, and score with the nonce gate (return 0 when the response omits the nonce, else strip the nonce from response and gold before `difflib.SequenceMatcher`). Re-pin `EVALCHEMY.commit` in `external_dependencies.py`.
2. Add `experiments/evaluation/configs/evalchemy/mrcr.yaml` selecting the task with `generation: true`, `completion_only: true` (base model → completions, not chat), greedy decoding (`temperature=0` via `extra_gen_kwargs`), and `max_length` matching the server's advertised context.
3. Run the bounded smoke against `snowball` through the served-evalchemy launcher, selecting one example per length-bin × needle-count cell that fits context, and persist raw prompts, generations, per-sample scores, prefix-hit rate, and cell coverage.

**Two decisions to settle before implementation**

- Cell-stratified "one example per length-bin × needle-count cell that fits context": implement inside the fork's dataset filter, or as a Marin-side sampler feeding `limit`? Context-fit depends on the served `max_length`, which argues for the task owning it.
- Artifact capture: confirm the fork's MRCR task emits per-sample logs the existing `lm_eval_samples` path can read, so prefix-hit rate and cell coverage roll up without a bespoke writer.

Once the fork task and a preferred split of the two decisions are agreed, the Marin side (dependency re-pin + `mrcr.yaml`) is small; the fork task and the CoreWeave smoke are the substantive work.

issues.author: muchanem
issues.body:
Sub-issue of #8366 (item 2). `load_parquet_batch` decodes every row group that overlaps its row range, then applies `filter_expr` with `table.filter` (`lib/zephyr/src/zephyr/readers.py:312`). There is no statistics-based row-group pruning, no page-index pruning, and no in-decoder filtering. #4344 chose this deliberately to fix the pyarrow.dataset memory blowup (#4325) and measured the cost: 0.17s vs 0.01s for a selective filter on a small column subset. A DataFusion-backed reader restores pushdown and retires pyarrow reader bugs we have hit (#5334 page headers over 8 MiB, apache/arrow#39808, #4586).

Plan:

- Swap at the `InputFileSpec` -> RecordBatch boundary. `_compute_file_pushdown` (`plan.py:517`) and the pipeline API do not change.
- One datafusion-python `SessionContext` per worker subprocess, configured like finelog's engine (`lib/finelog/rust/src/query/mod.rs:227`): `pushdown_filters` and `reorder_filters` on, a memory pool sized from the Iris task allocation so a bad scan fails with `ResourcesExhausted` instead of OOM-killing the worker, a parquet metadata cache, `repartition_file_min_size` lowered from the 10 MiB default.
- A `to_datafusion_expr` lowering for the `zephyr.expr` AST, beside `evaluate` and `to_pyarrow_expr`.
- One `register_object_store` per bucket using the CoreWeave contract from finelog's deployer (`lib/finelog/src/finelog/deploy/_k8s.py:158`): bucket spliced into the endpoint host, region `auto`, virtual-hosted addressing. Credentials come from the same rigging config the fsspec path reads.
- Intra-file row order is preserved; consumers assert it (sorted merge joins, `verify_fuzzy_dups`). Scan repartitioning is pinned accordingly.
- A backend enum selects pyarrow or datafusion during development and review only. After review the switch is wholesale and the pyarrow path is deleted. Deletion is gated on row-sliced specs (`approx_shard_bytes` spans): datafusion-python cannot select row groups today, so those specs need a PyO3 shim or an upstream change first.

Spikes before the implementation PRs:

1. Scan `s3://marin-us-east-*` through datafusion-python. cwobject.com accepts virtual-hosted addressing only, and finelog never scans S3 through its query context, so this path is unproven here. Fallback is the `object_store` env contract; failure reroutes the project to a PyO3 extension (`lib/dupekit` precedent).
2. Wheel coverage for every machine type we run: x86_64 (cw-rno2a and cw-us-east-02a GPU and CPU pools), aarch64 (cw-us-east-08a Grace), macOS arm64 dev machines. A missing wheel means a Rust toolchain build in every Iris worker venv.
3. A single-file microbenchmark: full scan at parity, a selective predicate winning, and a `pushdown_filters` regression check (5 of 43 ClickBench queries got slower even after the arrow-rs page-cache fix).

Benchmarks: tier 1 extends `lib/zephyr/tests/benchmark_parquet_reader.py` with a synthetic corpus sweeping row-group size, filter-column clustering, selectivity, and projection width. Tier 2 extends `experiments/datakit/zephyr_benchmark.py` over `sample_0.1b_7d7d8fd7` and `sample_100b_8ae7a94f`, one Iris job per workload and config point. Workloads: normalize, the common_corpus language/open-type predicate, the minhash two-column scan, scatter-chunk reads, the consolidate attribute join, and the global exact-dedup id scan. Each run records wall clock, bytes fetched, GET count, peak RSS, and DataFusion's `row_groups_pruned_statistics` counters.

Regression tests: a three-way differential asserting `evaluate`, `to_pyarrow_expr`, and `to_datafusion_expr` select identical rows on generated tables, with null semantics pinned by test; spec parity across backends (filter-column widening, row ranges, `include_file_paths`, row order); a golden-file corpus where the #5334 repro passes; the #4325 RSS bound kept green.

Scope: reader backend only. The SQL surface stays with #7686, distributed DataFusion with #7588, Polars pipeline internals with #8154/#8256. #5861 proposed a SQL loader and was declined; this issue stays below that line. Automatic lambda lowering is tracked in #8416 and projection inference in #8417. Landing is a stacked PR series at the end of the campaign.

Done when:
The DataFusion reader lands, the differential/parity/corpus suites run in unit CI, the benchmark report over the six workloads is posted here, and the pyarrow path is removed.
