spillover_issues.title: [rl] Pre-RL Snowball probe on R2E-Gym

spillover_issues.author: rjpower
spillover_issues.body:
## TL;DR

Just kicking off: measure whether adaptive environment/problem sampling improves RL training efficiency under a fixed compute budget, versus uniform random sampling.

## Description

We run SkyRL GRPO post-training on a small Qwen policy (0.6B class) over a pool of verifiable, non-agentic environments (math datasets spanning difficulty, plus simple programmatic tasks). Each arm uses the same model, data pool, and budget; only the policy for choosing which environment/problem to roll out next differs.

Arms:

1. Naive sampling: uniform random over the pool (baseline).
2. Modified Thompson sampling: bias toward environments currently yielding reward signal (e.g. per-env reward variance / pass-rate entropy), with decay so the belief tracks policy drift.
3. Pre-graded difficulty (problems graded 0–N easiest→hardest):
   - Naive curriculum: 1/N of budget per level.
   - Adaptive curriculum: train on a level until it stops paying (saturated or not learning), then move.
   - Biased sampling: grades seed an initial belief distribution for the Thompson sampler.

Budget: fixed output-token count per run, falling back to GPU wall-time (64 H100s x fixed hours) if token accounting is impractical. Runs use INTERACTIVE priority on cw-rno2a. The experiment is wired through Marin artifact steps (`marin.rl.skyrl`) so arms are cached and rerunnable; sampler support lands on a MarinSkyRL branch if the pinned trainer lacks the hooks.

## Hypothesis or Goal

Reward-signal-aware sampling concentrates rollouts where the learning signal is, so adaptive arms should reach a given eval score with fewer output tokens than uniform sampling. Quantify the value of each mechanism at fixed budget.

## Status

Kickoff. Wiring the experiment directory and a small smoke run.

Planned milestones, posted as comments:

1. Initial smoke run working end to end.
2. Curriculum/sampling infrastructure wired.
3. Results per sampling arm.
4. Final report on arm efficacy and follow-up recommendations.

## Links

* Logbook:
* W&B Report:
* Important updates:

## Decision Log

## Conclusion

comments.author: rjpower
comments.body:
🤖 Wiring status: the training loop works end to end; the smoke milestone is blocked only on a MarinSkyRL export bug.

What ran: `experiments/post_training/curriculum_rl/` builds a 6-bin graded pool (GSM8K, MATH L1-2/3/4/5, AIME 1983-2024; 10,427 train rows, 756 validation rows), mirrors Qwen/Qwen3-0.6B@c1899de, and runs SkyRL GRPO on 2 nodes of cw-rno2a H100s at interactive priority through `skyrl_step`, with pool/model artifacts cached across attempts. The smoke run completed all 4 GRPO steps over the mixed-env parquet (per-row `env_class`), logging per-environment metrics (train `environment/acc` 0.023 at step 4 — the raw 0.6B policy under a 1024-token cap).

Fixes landed on the branch along the way:

1. MarinSkyRL pin b45a6ed2 crashed at startup (`SKYRL_DEBUG_ARTIFACT_DIR is required`); advanced to d018d672, which contains the upstream fix.
2. The `aime` env asserts `extras["reward_model"]["ground_truth"]` (the gsm8k env reads `reward_spec`); pool rows now carry both columns.
3. The `aime` env verifies with the Minerva `Answer: ...` extraction, not `\boxed{}`; prompts now elicit a final Answer line. Representative ground truths (integers, degrees, fractions, tuples, radicals, polynomials) pass the skyrl-gym contract's two-sided preflight.

Open blocker: at d018d672 the terminal policy export (`cloud.iris.export_hf_checkpoint`) dies with `ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'torch'` — `skyrl_train/hf_export.py` pulls `skyrl_train.utils`, whose package init imports torch, into the deliberately torch-free launcher env. A fix branch (`fix-hf-export-torch-free`: move the torch-free `utils/io` subpackage and checkpoint-listing helpers out of the torch-bound `utils` package) is in progress; next smoke rerun follows it.

Confidence: high that the remaining blocker is isolated to export; the curriculum sampler infrastructure (MarinSkyRL `data.sampling` subtree + stateful weighted sampler) is being implemented in parallel.

comments.author: rjpower
comments.body:
🤖 Milestone 1: the smoke run is green end to end.

`/power/curriculum-rl-smoke-coord-r7` completed the full chain on cw-rno2a: graded-pool build → Qwen3-0.6B mirror → 2-node SkyRL GRPO (4 steps over the mixed six-bin parquet) → terminal HF export (`global_step_4`) → gsm8k-smoke eval, all as cached artifact steps at version 2026.08.29.1. Wall time for the RL step is about 10 minutes; the smoke score itself carries no signal at 4 steps.

Two more MarinSkyRL export bugs surfaced and were fixed on `fix-hf-export-torch-free` (now pinned at 5f6aed2d) beyond the torch-free import: the export subprocess wrote its console output to the launcher's JSON-only stdout, and it resolved the caller-relative cluster config from the wrong working directory. One experiment-side footgun: the launcher auto-defaults `trainer.hf_hub_repo_id` to `laion/<job_name>` and the export 403s creating that repo; arms now override it to null so exports stay in object storage.

Next: land the curriculum sampler branch (in progress), validate the thompson arm at smoke scale, then start the full 64-GPU naive baseline.

comments.author: rjpower
comments.body:
🤖 **Milestone 2: infrastructure wired for curricula & sampling.**

The curriculum sampler is implemented on MarinSkyRL branch [`curriculum-sampling`](https://github.com/marin-community/MarinSkyRL/tree/curriculum-sampling) (@2a9034fd) and validated live: naive, thompson, and grade-adaptive smoke arms all ran green end-to-end (train → HF export → eval) on cw-rno2a.

Design: a `data.sampling` config subtree selects a stateful weighted sampler over the pool's graded bins (`extra_info.data_source` / `grade`). Kinds: `naive` (stock shuffle), `thompson` (Beta posterior on the decay-weighted fraction of *informative* GRPO groups — groups whose rollout rewards are not all equal), `grade-uniform` (equal budget per grade), `grade-adaptive` (train one grade until its informative fraction stays below a threshold for a window, then advance), `grade-prior` (Thompson seeded with grade-derived optimism). The sampler is checkpoint-resumable (torchdata Stateful) and rejects duplicate rows per batch to preserve the GRPO group invariant.

Smoke evidence the machinery works (4-step runs, Qwen3-0.6B, non-thinking):
- thompson: weights collapsed to ~1% on the two bins with zero informative groups (MATH-L5, AIME) and concentrated on informative middle bins.
- grade-adaptive: 80% mass on grade 0 (gsm8k, informative_frac 0.47 — not yet exhausted, level correctly held at 0) with 20% exploration.
- Non-thinking mode fixed the truncation problem: 85% → 20% truncated, 4% → 70% parseable answers, ~500 avg output tokens.

Fixes along the way: unstepped-episode metrics crash, over-length prompts filtered at pool build (8 rows dropped), per-token reward scalarization for the sampler, batch-unique draws.

Next: full-scale arms (64 GPUs, 120 steps × 512 prompts × 8 samples each) starting with the naive baseline.

comments.author: rjpower
comments.body:
🤖 **Results: all five arms complete** (120 GRPO steps each, Qwen3-0.6B, 8×H100x8 per arm, cw-rno2a).

**Fixed output-token budget (146M generated tokens — the smallest arm's total):** last in-run validation eval at or under budget, avg_score on val-math500 / val-gsm8k:

| arm | tokens at eval | val-math500 | val-gsm8k |
|---|---|---|---|
| grade-adaptive | 146M (its full run) | **0.156** | 0.770 |
| thompson | 142M (~57% of run) | 0.140 | 0.758 |
| grade-uniform | 141M | 0.088 | 0.734 |
| naive | 136M (~50% of run) | 0.080 | **0.793** |
| grade-prior | 139M | 0.064 | 0.789 |

**Fixed step count (120 steps, unequal token spend):** terminal Evalchemy on the exported checkpoints:

| arm | total gen tokens | MATH500 acc | gsm8k-0shot (flexible) |
|---|---|---|---|
| naive | 274M | **0.460** | 0.450 |
| thompson | 251M | 0.412 | **0.516** |
| grade-uniform | 285M | 0.430 | 0.375 |
| grade-prior | 253M | 0.428 | 0.449 |
| grade-adaptive | 146M | 0.364 | 0.472 |

Base non-thinking Qwen3-0.6B started near val-math500 ≈ 0 and gsm8k ≈ 0.65, so every arm learns substantially. Wall time was ~1.75h for every arm (generation runs on fixed engine capacity), so fixed-step is also approximately fixed-GPU-hours: 5 arms × 64 GPU × 1.75h.

Reading: curriculum arms buy **token efficiency, not a better endpoint at equal steps**. grade-adaptive matched or beat the mid-run baselines while generating 53% of naive's tokens (it trains mostly on easier, shorter problems until they stop being informative); thompson tracks close behind and reallocates automatically without pre-grading. When the budget is steps/wall-time rather than tokens, naive remains the strongest MATH500 arm and thompson the strongest gsm8k arm.

Caveats: single seed per arm; 0.6B model; in-run val scorer (reward incl. penalties) differs from Evalchemy accuracy; grade-adaptive had not yet advanced past mid grades at 120 steps, so longer runs may shift the picture.

Final report with recommendations follows.

comments.author: rjpower
comments.body:
🤖 **Final report: efficacy and recommendations.**

**Conclusions.**
1. *Curriculum value here is token efficiency, not a better endpoint.* At a fixed generated-token budget (146M), grade-adaptive reached mid-run-baseline quality at ~53% of naive's token spend (val-math500 0.156 vs 0.080), with thompson close behind (0.140). At a fixed step/GPU-hour budget — where generation capacity is already paid for — naive was the best MATH500 arm (0.460) and thompson the best gsm8k arm (0.516); no curriculum dominated naive.
2. *Thompson sampling is the best no-prep default.* No offline grading required, decay handles policy drift, competitive under both budget definitions, and it visibly reallocated: bins with zero informative groups (MATH L5, AIME — all-fail for a 0.6B policy) dropped to the 1% floor.
3. *Grade-prior and grade-uniform added little* — the grade-derived prior washes out once real reward evidence accumulates, and fixed 1/N allocation wastes budget on uninformative extremes.

**Recommendations.**
- Re-run naive / thompson / grade-adaptive at 3 seeds for error bars before production conclusions (~$3 × current spend; each arm is 64 GPUs × 1.75 h).
- Extend grade-adaptive to 300+ steps so it traverses all grades; its curve was still rising at half the token budget.
- Make thompson difficulty-directional (distinguish all-pass from all-fail groups) — that should recover grade-adaptive's token efficiency without pre-grading.
- Batch-level uninformative-group resampling (DAPO-style) is complementary to bin-level sampling and likely stacks.

**Artifacts.** Sampler: MarinSkyRL `curriculum-sampling` @ 2a9034fd (checkpoint-resumable `data.sampling` subtree; worth PRing to main after multi-seed validation). Experiment: `experiments/post_training/curriculum_rl/` (PR to follow). Runs and curves: W&B project `marin-community/marin-curriculum-rl`; exported checkpoints under `s3://marin-us-east-02a/marin/users/power/checkpoints/curriculum-rl/<arm>/2026.08.29/exports/global_step_120`.

comments.author: rjpower
comments.body:
🤖 **Round 2 starting.** Scope, per review of round-1 results:

1. **DAPO dynamic sampling** — the pinned trainer already ships `trainer.algorithm.dynamic_sampling` (filter/replace with cross-batch accumulation); wiring it as arm variants (naive+dapo, thompson+dapo). One fix needed first: the curriculum-stat update must run before the filter, or every bin looks 100% informative to the sampler.
2. **Prior-sensitive pool** — round 1's grade-prior collapsed to thompson because 120 steps × 512 prompts of reward evidence swamps any prior over just 6 bins. Adding procedurally generated reasoning-gym bins (arithmetic chains, etc.) whose difficulty knobs give *genuine a-priori grades* and widen the bin count, so priors have room to matter. The reasoning-gym scorers only award 1.0 for a bare exact answer (full CoT responses get length-fuzz partial credit), so the env gets Minerva-style `Answer:`-line extraction first.
3. **Directional sampler** — new `learnability` kind: Thompson on per-bin pass rate, weight ∝ sampled p(1−p), which peaks at 50% solve rate and down-weights both all-pass and all-fail bins directionally (round-1 thompson treated them identically). `grade-prior` v2 seeds this posterior with grade-decreasing prior pass rates, so the prior is used directionally instead of as undirected optimism.
4. **Dropped:** grade-uniform (no signal over its simpler relatives in round 1).

Round-2 arms: naive, thompson, learnability, grade-prior(directional), grade-adaptive, naive+dapo, thompson+dapo — same fixed budgets and eval protocol as round 1.

comments.author: rjpower
comments.body:
🤖 **Round 2 infrastructure wired; smoke green.** All four follow-ups are implemented and validated end-to-end on cw-rno2a (`/power/curriculum-rl-r2-smoke2`):

- **DAPO** — `trainer.algorithm.dynamic_sampling.type=filter` wired as arm variants `naive-dapo` / `thompson-dapo`. The curriculum sampler now updates on **raw pre-filter batches** (MarinSkyRL `9a7286b4`); previously it would have run post-filter and read every bin as 100% informative. Smoke shows the filter engaging: 33–50/64 prompts informative per raw batch, one resample batch per step.
- **Prior-sensitive datasets** — pool v3 adds seven procedurally generated reasoning-gym bins (chain_sum ×3, spell_backward ×2, base_conversion ×2; 1,200 rows each) whose difficulty knobs give genuine a-priori grades, interleaved with the re-graded math bins on a shared 0–10 scale. The `reasoning_gym` env scores only the final `Answer:` line (`d36ceaaa`) — full CoT responses previously got ~0.05 fuzz credit even when correct. Smoke pass rates confirm the machinery and expose grade-placement surprises to analyze at full scale (chain_sum-med ~0.9 at grade 3; spell-backward ~0.15–0.33 vs math-l12 ~0.03 — spelling is easier for the base model than its grade assumed).
- **Directional sampler** — new `learnability` kind: Thompson draw on each bin's decayed pass rate, weighted by p·(1−p), peaking at 50% solve rate so it distinguishes too-easy from too-hard (the informative-group signal alone cannot). `grade-prior` is redefined as its grade-seeded variant: prior pass-rate mean falls linearly from 0.85 (easiest grade) to 0.05 (hardest) with pseudo-count `grade_prior_strength` (`0b44138c`).
- **Grade-uniform dropped** from the arm catalog.

Launching round-2 full arms next: naive, thompson, learnability, grade-adaptive, grade-prior, naive-dapo, thompson-dapo — 120 steps × 64 H100s each on the expanded pool.

comments.author: rjpower
comments.body:
🤖 # Round 2 final report: DAPO, procedural bins, and directional samplers

All seven arms completed: 120 GRPO steps each on 64 H100s (cw-rno2a, Qwen3-0.6B, batch 512×8 samples, non-thinking, ~1024-token generations). Every arm shares the same expanded pool and differs only in prompt sampling and (for the DAPO variants) group filtering. Terminal evals are Evalchemy MATH500 and GSM8K-0shot against the exported step-120 checkpoint; in-run validation is scored by the training environments on held-out slices.

## Results

| arm | generated tokens | in-run val (all) | MATH500 | GSM8K-0shot |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| naive | 203M | 0.513 | 0.362 | 0.390 |
| thompson | 149M | 0.480 | 0.350 | 0.409 |
| learnability | 220M | 0.537 | 0.418 | 0.444 |
| grade-adaptive | 130M | 0.534 | 0.346 | 0.439 |
| grade-prior (directional) | 211M | 0.487 | 0.408 | 0.418 |
| naive-dapo | 190M | 0.555 | 0.414 | 0.401 |
| **thompson-dapo** | 205M | **0.571** | **0.434** | **0.456** |

Token totals include work redone after preemption-driven restarts (real spend). Round-2 numbers are not comparable to round 1: the pool now spends a large share of budget on procedural bins, which lowers math transfer for every arm equally (round-1 naive hit 0.460 MATH500 on the math-only pool).

![score vs tokens](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/marin-community/marin/assets/curriculum-rl-r2/all-tokens.png)
![score vs steps](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/marin-community/marin/assets/curriculum-rl-r2/all-steps.png)

MATH500 and GSM8K validation trajectories against token spend:

![val-math500 vs tokens](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/marin-community/marin/assets/curriculum-rl-r2/val-math500-tokens.png)
![val-gsm8k vs tokens](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/marin-community/marin/assets/curriculum-rl-r2/val-gsm8k-tokens.png)

## Grading mechanism and distributions

Grades place all 13 bins on one 0–10 scale from two sources. Math bins take grades from **source metadata**: GSM8K at 1, MATH levels 1–2/3/4/5 at 2/4/6/8, AIME at 10. Procedural reasoning-gym bins take **a-priori grades from generator knobs**, assigned before any model saw a sample: chain_sum at grades 0/3/7 (2 terms 1–2 digits → 5–6 terms 4 digits signed), spell_backward at 5/9 (3–5 vs 8–10 letters), base_conversion at 5/9 (bases 2–10 values ≤500 vs bases 11–16). Train pool: 18,619 rows (gsm8k 2000, math-l12 1911, math-l3 1590, math-l4 1690, math-l5 2296, aime 932, 7 procedural bins × 1200); validation adds 128-row held-out generator draws per procedural family.

How well did the grades predict reality? Realized pass rates from the learnability arm:

| bin (grade) | pass rate @ step 10 | @ step 120 |
|---|---|---|
| rg-sum-easy (0) | 0.97 | 1.00 |
| gsm8k (1) | 0.49 | 0.84 |
| math-l12 (2) | 0.53 | 0.84 |
| rg-sum-med (3) | 0.97 | 0.99 |
| math-l3 (4) | 0.41 | 0.70 |
| rg-spell-short (5) | 0.82 | 1.00 |
| rg-base-small (5) | 0.58 | 0.90 |
| math-l4 (6) | 0.28 | 0.57 |
| rg-sum-hard (7) | 0.74 | 0.90 |
| math-l5 (8) | 0.07 | 0.27 |
| rg-base-large (9) | 0.26 | 0.96 |
| rg-spell-long (9) | 0.79 | 0.97 |
| aime (10) | 0.00 | 0.06 |

Two clear findings. **Within a family, metadata grades rank difficulty essentially perfectly** (math: 0.53 → 0.41 → 0.28 → 0.07 → 0.004 down the levels). **Across families, knob-derived grades misjudged absolute difficulty badly**: arithmetic chains are near-trivial for Qwen3-0.6B at any knob setting we chose, and spelling/base-conversion saturate within ~10 steps once the model learns the answer format — procedural tasks measure format acquisition more than reasoning. The pre-registered grades were wrong in exactly the way a real practitioner's would be, which made this a fair test of whether samplers recover from miscalibrated priors.

## Sampling mechanisms

- **naive** — the stock uniform shuffle without replacement. Control.
- **thompson** — Beta Thompson sampling on each bin's decayed *informative-group fraction* (a GRPO group is informative when its rewards are not all equal), decay 0.95, 5% probability floor. Round 1's design.
- **learnability** (new) — Thompson draw on each bin's decayed per-sample *pass rate*, weighted by p·(1−p), which peaks at 50% solve rate. Motivated by round 1's core diagnosis: informative-fraction cannot distinguish a too-easy bin from a too-hard one (both produce uniform groups), so it has no direction.
- **grade-prior** (redesigned) — learnability with grade-seeded Beta priors: prior mean pass rate falls linearly from 0.85 at the easiest grade to 0.05 at the hardest, with 8 pseudo-counts. Round 1's undirected-optimism version collapsed to thompson within ~20 steps; this version encodes the grade as a belief about *pass rate*, which the p·(1−p) weighting turns into "start in the middle band."
- **grade-adaptive** — a level pointer walking the grade ladder, advancing when the current level stops producing informative signal; 20% exploration mass off-level.
- **DAPO filter** (`naive-dapo`, `thompson-dapo`) — drop zero-advantage groups after generation and keep drawing batches until a full informative batch accumulates (the standard DAPO dynamic-sampling recipe). The curriculum sampler updates on raw pre-filter batches so filtering does not bias its statistics.

Weight trajectories show the directional machinery working as designed. Learnability zeroes the saturated procedural bins almost immediately, holds AIME near the floor, and walks its mass up the math ladder as the model improves (math-l3/l4 dominate late). Grade-prior starts mid-band per its prior, then evidence overrides the miscalibrated procedural placements within ~15 steps:

![learnability weights](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/marin-community/marin/assets/curriculum-rl-r2/curriculum-learnability-weight.png)
![grade-prior weights](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/marin-community/marin/assets/curriculum-rl-r2/curriculum-grade-prior-weight.png)

## Analysis

1. **DAPO is the single biggest win.** thompson-dapo leads every metric, and both DAPO arms beat their non-DAPO counterparts at *equal token spend*, not just equal steps — filtering converts budget that would fund zero-gradient groups into informative ones. The score-vs-tokens chart shows the DAPO curves rising fastest through the whole budget range.
2. **Direction matters more than curriculum-ness.** Learnability (0.418/0.444) beats thompson (0.350/0.409) decisively — same Thompson machinery, better signal. Plain thompson was the weakest arm, confirming round 1's suspicion that informative-fraction is a compass without a needle.
3. **Grades survive contact with reality only where they were right.** Grade-prior recovered from its miscalibrated procedural priors but paid an early-budget tax for them, landing between thompson and learnability. With honest grades (the math family) the ordering is genuinely useful; with guessed grades the evidence-driven samplers simply relearn the truth and the prior contributes little. Grading effort is only worth what the grader knows.
4. **Grade-adaptive remains the token-efficiency champion** (0.534 val-all on 130M tokens, ~64% of naive's spend), echoing round 1. Its focused single-level sampling generates shorter, more solvable rollouts.
5. **Procedural tasks are cheap curriculum filler but weak transfer vehicles.** They gave the samplers real difficulty structure to exploit and clean val curves (e.g. base-conversion 0.26→0.96), but every arm's MATH500 dropped versus round 1's math-only pool. At 0.6B, budget spent on spelling does not buy math.

## Conclusions and future work

At fixed budget, the value ranking is: DAPO filtering > directional (pass-rate) sampling > adaptive level curricula > grade priors > informative-fraction sampling. The obvious composition — **learnability + DAPO** — was not run this round and is the first follow-up: the mechanisms are orthogonal (what to sample vs what to keep) and their gains plausibly stack.

Future work, in priority order:
- **learnability-dapo arm** at the same budget point.
- **Measured grades over guessed grades**: a ~1-hour pre-pass scoring k samples per bin with the base model would have produced a nearly perfect prior for free; grade-prior with measured priors is the honest test of "grades as belief."
- **Token-budget-equalized stopping** (stop every arm at, say, 150M generated tokens) to remove the step/token conflation entirely.
- **A model one size up** (4–8B, thinking mode) where AIME-band bins are learnable and the grade ladder has more headroom.
- Infra hardening from this round is tracked separately: #8774 (gang restart after head preemption, in progress), #8781/#8782 (TAS priority preemption, merged), plus the eval endpoint queue-time fix and TTL-routed Ray session logs in #8769.

Experiment code and pins are in #8769 (`experiments/post_training/curriculum_rl/`, MarinSkyRL `curriculum-sampling` @ `4a1f99fc`). Charts regenerate with `report_charts.py`; per-bin stats with `report_pool_stats.py`; terminal scores with `report_evals.py`.

comments.author: rjpower
comments.body:
🤖 Round-3 finding: adaptive sampling is fragile to reward-contract mismatch; grade priors buy robustness.

The snowball-learnability-dapo arm showed val-gsm8k pass@1 = 0.000 at step 10 while snowball-naive scored 0.891 from the same base model — with learnability simultaneously beating naive on harder bins (MATH-500 0.66 vs 0.63). Retained trajectories pin the cause: Snowball answers gsm8k correctly but in its SFT style (`\boxed{300}`), while the gsm8k environment's rule grader only accepts the answer after `"####"`, so every rollout scores 0. The bin's zero pass rate measures format compliance, not ability.

The three samplers then diverge exactly along their designs:

- **naive** samples gsm8k uniformly (~54 rollouts/step); rare rollouts that happen to emit `####` get positive advantage and RL teaches the format within 10 steps → val 0.891.
- **learnability + group-informative weighting** observes pass = 0 at step 1, assigns the bin near-floor weight (0.009 vs ~0.09 for active bins), starves it, and never learns the format → val 0.000.
- **grade-prior + group-informative** keeps sampling on its grade-3 prior (9 informative groups by step 9, pass EMA 0.16 → 0.33) and recovers → val 0.828 at step 10.

Letting the arms run to 60 steps as-is: the dynamics are the experiment. For the report, the snowball headline metric will be shown with and without val-gsm8k, since the bin conflates format with difficulty for this model. Follow-up recommendation: normalize every pool bin to one answer contract (`\boxed{}` + math-verify) so grades measure difficulty only, and add cold-start optimism or a re-exploration floor to pure-feedback samplers so an observed-zero bin is revisited often enough to distinguish "too hard" from "mis-specified".

comments.author: rjpower
comments.body:
🤖 Round-3 final report: graded-ladder curricula on Qwen3-0.6B and Snowball 67B-A2B.

All nine arms completed: six Qwen arms (120 steps, 64 H100s each, ~230–247M generated tokens) and three Snowball arms (60 steps, 64 H100s each, ~64–75M tokens) on the grade 0–13 math ladder, scored by the fixed end metric (validation pass@1 weighted by 1+grade, never visible to samplers).

| arm | grade-weighted | without gsm8k | frontier grade | tokens |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| qwen learnability-dapo | **0.312** | 0.266 | 9 | 247M |
| snowball grade-prior-dapo | **0.310** | 0.256 | **13** | 71M |
| qwen grade-prior-dapo | 0.301 | 0.255 | 9 | 245M |
| qwen naive-dapo | 0.294 | 0.248 | 5 | 229M |
| snowball naive | 0.289 | 0.232 | 5 | 64M |
| qwen grade-prior | 0.283 | 0.238 | 5 | 240M |
| qwen naive | 0.267 | 0.219 | 5 | 231M |
| qwen grade-adaptive | 0.257 | 0.211 | 5 | 144M |
| snowball learnability-dapo | 0.166 | 0.181 | 5 | 75M |

![grade-weighted score vs tokens](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/marin-community/marin/assets/curriculum-rl-r3/grade-weighted-tokens.png)

**Qwen: curriculum sampling wins cleanly.** Both group-informative curriculum arms beat plain DAPO, which beats everything else: learnability-dapo ends +17% relative over naive (0.312 vs 0.267) and +6% over naive-dapo. Only the two curriculum-DAPO arms pushed the frontier to grade 9 (AMC pass@1 ≥ 0.25); every other arm stalled at grade 5 (MATH). Grade-adaptive (ladder-walking) finished last and also spent the fewest tokens — it parks on easy bins with short responses.

![frontier grade vs tokens](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/marin-community/marin/assets/curriculum-rl-r3/frontier-grade-tokens.png)

**Snowball: grade priors won; pure feedback-driven sampling failed twice.** grade-prior-dapo reached 0.310 with frontier grade 13 (TheoremQA ≥ 0.25) in 71M tokens and was still improving at step 60. The learnability arm hit both failure modes:

1. *Format-contract starvation* (details in the [mid-run comment](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/8765#issuecomment-5471696465)): gsm8k pass@1 stayed 0.000 for the entire run because an observed zero pass rate zeroes the group-informative weight; naive learned the `####` contract by step 10 (0.94 final) and grade-prior recovered through its prior (0.95 final).
2. *Late-run collapse*: stable through step 50 (MATH-500 0.64–0.70, TheoremQA 0.25–0.28), then one destabilizing update at step 60 — raw grad-norm 19,332, KL-max 9.3, entropy 0.085 — dropped every bin (MATH-500 → 0.52), and the terminal export captured the damaged checkpoint. Snowball-naive also slid from its 0.324 mid-run peak to 0.289; only grade-prior-dapo ended at its peak. Single-seed caveat applies, but concentrated sampling appears to raise late-run variance.

![val-gsm8k vs tokens](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/marin-community/marin/assets/curriculum-rl-r3/val-gsm8k-tokens.png)

**The sampling objective checks out empirically.** Pooling per-bin pass-rate transitions across all curriculum arms, learning velocity peaks near pass rate 0.4–0.5 (~0.008/step) and falls to ~0 at both extremes — matching the flat-topped group-informative curve 1−pⁿ−(1−p)ⁿ more closely than p(1−p):

![learning velocity vs pass rate](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/marin-community/marin/assets/curriculum-rl-r3/velocity-vs-pass-rate.png)

**Infrastructure notes.** Snowball steps ran at ~8.8 min after raising `micro_train_batch_size_per_gpu` 1→4 (the FSDP update was all-gather-bound: 32 sequential re-gathers of 134GB shards for ~2B active params of compute; the fix cut policy_train 1660s→437s). Remaining round-3 ops incidents were all transient: one driver OOM at the default 1GB coordinator memory, one eval endpoint-registration timeout, one export stuck on an Iris pod race after its container completed.

**Recommendations for a round 4.**
- Normalize every bin to one answer contract (`\boxed{}` + math-verify) so grades measure difficulty, not instruction-style compliance.
- Give pure-feedback samplers cold-start optimism and a re-exploration floor that periodically re-probes zero-pass bins; without it they cannot distinguish "too hard" from "mis-specified".
- Default to grade priors when moving a curriculum to a new model: they were never worse than naive on any bin, on either model.
- Add a stability guard (KL trust region or late LR decay) for long runs under concentrated sampling; the step-60 blowup was visible in grad-norm before the eval caught it.

Full chart set and summary.json: [assets/curriculum-rl-r3](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/assets/curriculum-rl-r3).

comments.author: rjpower
comments.body:
🤖 Round 4 launched: `/power/curriculum-r4-full` on cw-us-east-02a — Snowball, `naive` vs `grade-prior-dapo`, 120 steps at pool version `2026.09.01.1`.

Changes from round 3:

- **Optimizer**: MuonH at lr 1e-5, weight_decay 0, grad clip 1.0 — the same recipe Snowball pretrained/SFT'd with. Round 3 used AdamW at 2e-6.
- **Batch shape**: 64 prompts × 8 samples × 120 steps (same rollout total as round 3's 60 bigger steps, 2× fresher policy), micro-batch 8 — halves the all-gather count that dominated round-3 step time.
- **Prompt contracts**: system prompt plus strengthened per-bin format instructions baked into the pool. Served-model A/B (temp 1.0, rule-graded, 100 problems/variant): gsm8k 0.00 → 0.55 and math500 0.05 → 0.15 before any RL; failures under the old prompts were correct math ending in `\boxed{}` instead of the graded answer line.
- **Curriculum**: the grade-prior-dapo arm adds `reversion_mass=2.0` — per-step pseudo-evidence that pulls starved bins back toward re-probeable weight, addressing the round-3 starvation self-lock (MarinSkyRL `129ed37a`).

Smoke (4 steps, MuonH + micro=8): step time 222s vs 534s in round 3, raw grad norm 0.38–0.47 under the 1.0 clip. At 222s/step the full arms should take ~7.5h each.

Next: monitor both arms to completion, verify think-token structure and truncation rates from retained trajectories, then the round-4 report.

comments.author: rjpower
comments.body:
🤖 Round 4 complete. Both Snowball arms ran 120 steps at `2026.09.01.1` (MuonH lr 1e-5, system prompt + strengthened format contracts, `reversion_mass=2.0` on the curriculum arm). The grade-prior-dapo arm finished in one attempt; naive hit two micro-batch-8 CUDA OOMs (steps 92 and 119) and resumed cleanly from checkpoint both times.

Final evals (round-3 in parentheses):

| arm | grade-weighted | frontier grade | metered tokens |
|---|---|---|---|
| naive | 0.285 (0.289) | 5 (5) | 89M |
| grade-prior-dapo | **0.292** (0.310) | **13** (13) | 81M |

Headlines:

- The prompt contract moved the format unlock out of RL: both arms hit val-gsm8k ≥ 0.89 at the first eval (step 10), and the naive-vs-curriculum composite gap shrank from +0.021 to +0.007. Most of round 3's curriculum margin was exposure to a format-deceptive bin; a two-paragraph prompt buys the same thing.
- The frontier edge is what survives: grade-prior-dapo again sustained the grade-13 bin (theoremqa 0.268, crossing ~75M tokens) while naive never did — the same 13-vs-5 split as round 3 under a different optimizer, batch shape, and prompt.
- MuonH at 5× the round-3 lr was stable end to end (grad norms 0.17–0.47 under the 1.0 clip, no late-run collapse), and micro-batch 8 halved step time (222s vs 534s).
- `reversion_mass` behaved as designed: all 19 bin weights stayed within a ~3× band; no floor-lock.
- Regression: peak val-math500 fell 0.656 → 0.562 in both arms (candidates: 512 vs 1024 rollouts/step, lr drift, or the anti-`\boxed{}` contract; unresolved at one seed).
- Retained-trajectory analysis: 40–48% of rollouts still hit the 2048-token cap at end of training; frontier bins truncate near-totally (AIME 98%, Omni 99%). Successful rollouts are short, ~100% think-token structured by step 100, and `\boxed{}` was ground out of successes entirely. Generation budget, not sampling, is now the binding constraint — top round-5 lever.

Paper (round-4 section added) and all figures: https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/assets/curriculum-rl-paper/paper.md

comments.author: rjpower
comments.body:
🤖 **Round 5 launched** (`/power/curriculum-r5-full`, version `2026.09.02.1`): naive + grade-prior-dapo, 120 steps × 64 prompts × 8 samples, with the round-4 recipe (MuonH 1e-5, clip 1.0, reversion_mass 2.0) and two changes:

- **Generation budget 2048 → 8192** (window 9216, same 1024-token prompt budget). Round 4's binding constraint: 40–48% of rollouts truncated at the cap, AIME/Omni/TheoremQA near-totally. `micro_train_batch_size_per_gpu` 8 → 2 to hold activation memory at the longer sequences.
- **System prompt 111 → 37 tokens.** Served-model A/B (temp 1.0, rule-graded, 100–250 rows/variant, strong per-bin suffixes held fixed):

  | system prompt | gsm8k comp/pass | math500 comp/pass | theoremqa comp/pass |
  |---|---|---|---|
  | current 111t | 0.79/0.38 | 0.60/0.16 | 0.42/0.04 |
  | tight 66t | 0.80/0.41 | 0.52/0.15 | 0.36/0.08 |
  | **minimal 37t** | 0.77/0.52 | 0.54/0.20 | 0.36/0.08 |

  Compliance is flat; pass ties or favors the shortest. Fixed overhead per request drops from 155 to ~81 tokens (of the 1024-token input window). Prompt tokens are unmetered and prefix-cached, so the win is window room, not compute.

Smoke (4 steps, same config): no OOM at micro=2, ~750 s/step (policy_train 455 s + generate 250 s), avg generation 3,000–4,200 tokens, truncation 19–36% on the pre-RL policy (vs 40–48% at end of round 4). Pool `2026.09.02.1`: 23,265 train rows, new prompt verified in-region. Expect ~27–30 h/arm; metered spend likely 2–3× round 4.

Open questions this round answers: does the 8192 budget open grades 11–12 (round 4: budget-starved, not merely hard), and does math500 recover from the 0.656 → 0.562 regression.

comments.author: rjpower
comments.body:
🤖 Round 5 (8192-token budget) — naive arm complete, dapo arm resumed after a crash.

**Naive arm: finished 120/120 steps** (~24.6 h, ~627 s/step, truncation ~0.25 vs 0.40–0.48 in round 4). 210.8M generated tokens (round-4 naive: 89M at the same step count — the longer budget spends ~2.4×). Step-120 in-training eval: math500 0.532, gsm8k 0.891, theoremqa 0.241, rg-sum 0.992, amc 0.070, omni 0.013. Post-RL eval stage is running now.

**Grade-prior-dapo arm: crashed at step 69** (attempt exit 250, connection refused to an inference-engine metrics endpoint — same failure signature as the round-4 crash). Iris auto-resubmitted; the run resumed from the step-69 checkpoint (exact-rev pin preserved the config hash) and is at step ~76 at ~1050 s/step. ETA roughly 13 h; DAPO redraws remain pricier per step at the long budget.

Charts and the round-5 report follow once the dapo arm and both eval stages finish.

comments.author: rjpower
comments.body:
🤖 Round 5 complete (8192-token budget) — final results, and the budget hypothesis is refuted.

| arm | grade-weighted | frontier | metered tokens | math500 (Evalchemy, 8192 eval cap) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| naive | 0.270 (r4: 0.285) | 5 | 211M | **0.656** |
| grade-prior-dapo | 0.280 (r4: 0.292) | 5 (r4: 13) | 260M† | 0.648 |

† includes steps retraced across two crash-resumes.

Three findings:

1. **The long budget cost 2.4× the tokens and returned a lower composite.** Truncation only fell to 0.25–0.35 — the model fills whatever room it gets (mean generation length drifted to ~8.2k by the end), and answer-line hygiene slipped (val-gsm8k 0.934 → 0.891).
2. **Round 4's math500 regression was an eval artifact.** At an 8192-token *evaluation* cap, both round-5 checkpoints score ~0.65 on math500 — matching round 3's peak. Round 4's 0.562 came from a 2048-token eval cap truncating long solutions. Evaluate generous, even when training tight.
3. **DAPO's edge is a short-budget phenomenon.** At matched token or wall budgets the gap is ≤0.01 and the frontier split (13 vs 5 in rounds 3–4) vanished. Redraws pay by replacing truncation-manufactured all-fail groups; at 8192 those mostly don't exist, while dapo still costs 1.7×/step (~1.3×/token). Grades 11+ never opened (amc ≤0.117, omni ≤0.027) — capability, not budget, binds the frontier at this checkpoint.

Recommendation after five rounds: **train at a modest generation budget (where the grade prior + DAPO buy ~2 frontier grades at equal tokens), evaluate at a generous one.** Next lever is per-instance selection (retire mastered problems, replay frontier ones) on the RowStats evidence already upstream.

Paper §8 with charts: https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/assets/curriculum-rl-paper/paper.md — experiment package merged in #8769, sampling stack upstream in marin-community/MarinSkyRL#470, endpoint-wait fix in #8866.

spillover_issues.author: mcwitt
spillover_issues.body:
`levanter.grug._moe` marks the whole package private in its `__init__.py` ("Private Grug MoE backend implementations"), and then prefixes names inside it with an underscore as well. Thirty-seven of those names are imported by a module other than the one that defines them, so the marker says module-private about names that are never used module-privately.

`_zero_inactive_grouped_rows` is the clearest case. It is defined in `_moe/common.py` and used five times in `_moe/sonic_cute.py`, and never in the module that defines it.

The names span thirteen modules:

```
sharding.py                          9    ep_deepep.py                        1
ep_common.py                         9    ep_fixed_all_to_all.py              1
common.py                            6    ep_fixed_pooled_wave_all_to_all.py  1
sonic_cute.py                        4    ep_ragged_all_to_all.py             1
cudnn_wgrad_cute.py                  1    ep_ring.py                          1
local.py                             1    scatter.py                          1
sonic.py                             1
```

Some cross a distribution boundary, not just a module one. `lib/marin/src/marin/testing/moe/ragged_ep.py` imports `_clip_receiver_group_sizes`, `_EXPERT_CHUNKS`, `_quack_grouped_gemm_available`, and `_select_expert_mlp` from levanter, and `tests/test_grug_variant_contracts.py` imports `_compact_grug_mesh_shape`. A leading underscore is the only signal Python has for "do not import this", and marin imports them anyway.

The prefix also costs the thing it was meant to buy. Because everything is underscored, the package cannot distinguish a helper genuinely local to one module from one that is part of the package's internal interface. `_moe/sharding.py` and `_moe/ep_common.py` are effectively shared libraries for the backends, and nothing in the naming says so.

Dropping the prefix from names that cross module boundaries inside `_moe/` leaves the package private via its path, which is where privacy is already enforced. It is mechanical: every importer is in this repository, there are no dynamic lookups by name, and the compatibility rule in `AGENTS.md` says to update call sites rather than keep aliases. It is wide, though, which is why it does not belong inside a feature PR — #8549 added six such names by following the surrounding style, and the reviewer noticed the style rather than the change.

Raised in review on #8549: https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/8549#discussion_r3876485352

Done when:

- Names in `levanter.grug._moe` that are imported by another module no longer carry a leading underscore, and names used only within their defining module still do.
- Importers are updated in place, in `lib/levanter`, `lib/marin`, `tests/`, and `experiments/`, with no compatibility aliases.
- `uv run --no-project infra/ci/run_tests.py` passes, and `./infra/pre-commit.py --all-files` is clean.

spillover_issues.body:
## TL;DR

[PR #8651](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/8651) replaces Polars inside Zephyr's shuffle with DataFusion, keeps Zephyr's external spill files on region-local GCS, and exposes DataFusion SQL for columnar map and reducer stages.

Against current main/Polars, the 13 SQL-migrated Datakit stages used 29.39% less CPU, 21.38% less summed stage time, and 49.93% less peak shard memory. Across all 16 shuffle-affected stages, including fuzzy verification's unchanged Python reducer, CPU fell 26.82%. Region-local output validators matched exactly.

## Description

The SQL API mirrors the efficiency boundaries established by [#8154](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/8154) and [#8256](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/8256):

- `Dataset.sql(...)` runs batch-local map queries against an `input` view.
- `Dataset.group_by(..., reducer=sql(...))` runs a query over the complete target shard after Zephyr's external merge.
- Scalar SQL functions provide expression-based routing keys without serializing DataFusion objects into a plan.

Datakit normalization, fuzzy graph construction, all connected-component iterations, and final fuzzy-attribute materialization use these paths. Fuzzy verification still uses the generic DataFusion shuffle with its existing Python reducer. Download, MinHash, memory-store loading, consolidation, tokenization, and cache-probe work do not execute the new SQL path.

DataFusion native disk spill stays disabled. Zephyr continues to write bounded sorted Parquet chunks and external merge runs to the stage filesystem, which is GCS on Iris. Eight target-shard ranges bound each DataFusion sort while preserving one selected file per mapper flush at reduce time.

## Hypothesis or Goal

Remove Zephyr's Polars dependency and use DataFusion for shuffle sorting, reading, and columnar map/reduce computation without changing semantic output, moving external spill off GCS, or retaining the original DataFusion memory and CPU regressions.

## Status

The implementation is complete on PR #8651, rebased on control commit `dc584e765d` with treatment head `fbddc9de28`.

The affected repository selection passed 1,529 tests with three skips and five expected failures. Ruff, Black, license checks, Pyrefly, documentation checks, and all remaining changed-file checks passed.

## Current-main Datakit ferry

Workload: FineWeb-Edu `sample/10BT` at revision `87f0914`, 14 input files, and the full `experiments.ferries.datakit_ferry` path used by the Polars columnar A/B. Both arms ran concurrently with identical non-preemptible resources in `europe-west4`. Inputs, outputs, status, caches, and Zephyr temporary files all used `gs://marin-eu-west4`; no cross-region GCS access was configured.

Control: main/Polars `dc584e765d`, [`/loom/zephyr-sql-ferry-20260828-control`](https://iris.oa.dev/#/job/%2Floom%2Fzephyr-sql-ferry-20260828-control), 56m11.18s.

Treatment: DataFusion SQL `fbddc9de28`, [`/loom/zephyr-sql-ferry-20260828-treatment`](https://iris.oa.dev/#/job/%2Floom%2Fzephyr-sql-ferry-20260828-treatment), 59m00.15s (+168.97s, +5.01%).

| Operation / stage | CPU control | CPU treatment | CPU change | Elapsed control | Elapsed treatment | Elapsed change |

The SQL-migrated stages processed the same 558,478,005 logical items; all shuffle-affected stages matched at 559,057,070. Byte telemetry is not comparable because the treatment counts Arrow buffer bytes while the control counts its row-oriented representation.

The [control validator](https://iris.oa.dev/#/job/%2Floom%2Fzephyr-sql-validate-20260828-control-v2) and [treatment validator](https://iris.oa.dev/#/job/%2Floom%2Fzephyr-sql-validate-20260828-treatment-v2) each found 9,672,101 downloaded rows, 9,268,156 normalized rows, 532,777 fuzzy cluster members with 246,814 representatives, 45,970 verified duplicates, and 9,222,186 consolidated and tokenized rows.

Measured CPU across the full ferry fell 9.04%, and summed stage time fell 4.09%. Root wall time rose 5.01% because unaffected runtime was noisier: tokenization elapsed rose from 333.92 to 474.38 seconds with CPU essentially unchanged at +0.69%, followed by a longer cache-probe scheduling delay. Unaffected-stage CPU was flat at -0.30%.

## Earlier evidence

The range-only DataFusion A/B, before the SQL path, used 5.25% more CPU than Polars across the 16 shuffle-affected stages while lowering peak shard memory 43.28%. That isolated Python row materialization and reducer callbacks as the remaining actionable cost.

A control-only Polars target-range sweep showed that the memory mechanism is engine-independent:

| Polars target ranges | Writer time | Change |
|---:|---:|---:|
| 1 (baseline) | 2.600 s | - |
| 2 | 2.649 s | +1.92% |
| 4 | 2.770 s | +6.55% |
| 8 | 3.319 s | +27.69% |

| 1 (baseline) | 1.434 GB | - |

An earlier pre-optimization Nemotron A/B raised affected-stage CPU 39.99% and peak memory from 7.88 to 13.42 GB. That run identified the original whole-buffer DataFusion `SortExec` problem and does not represent the current range-partitioned SQL treatment.

## Links

- Implementation and review: [PR #8651](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/8651)
- Per-stage A/B and historical detail: [sticky PR comment](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/8651#issuecomment-5403476301)
- Root-cause and benchmark investigation: [Echo record](https://echo.oa.dev/wiki/267)

## Decision Log

- DataFusion native disk spill stays disabled so its internal sorter remains in memory.
- Zephyr's explicit sorted chunks and external merge intermediates remain on the stage filesystem and therefore use region-local GCS on Iris.
- DataFusion uses eight target-shard ranges because two exhausted the sorter and four retained materially more memory.
- SQL is exposed as a serializable Zephyr plan object instead of exposing DataFusion runtime objects.
- Datakit uses SQL only where the transformation is columnar; fuzzy verification retains Python callbacks for full-text comparison and side effects.

## Conclusion

The Python implementation removes the DataFusion memory and CPU regressions without modifying DataFusion. On the matched Datakit ferry, SQL-migrated DataFusion stages were faster than current-main Polars while using half the peak shard memory, and persisted outputs matched exactly.

spillover_issues.author: dlwh
spillover_issues.body:
## Description

Evaluate whether June 67B context-extension checkpoints use retained MRCR conversation context when scoring the same final assistant response. The paired evaluator compares `full_context` with `query_only`, scores response-body tokens, and stratifies deterministic bootstrap intervals by needle count and evidence distance.

## Task

An MRCR source document contains two worked examples, a long multi-turn conversation with 2, 4, or 8 relevant facts ("needles"), and a final query. `desired_msg_index` identifies a user request in that conversation; its matching answer is the immediately following assistant message.

Each source row produces two documents with the same final query and gold response:

```text
full_context: two worked examples + target conversation + final query -> gold response
query_only:   two worked examples + final query                       -> gold response
```

The primary two-shot prompt supplies the benchmark's 10-character answer prefix. The evaluator scores only the remaining gold assistant response body. The worked examples, retained conversation, final query, supplied prefix, and EOS are context and receive zero loss. Each condition occupies one unsliced, unpacked sequence.

The paired comparison asks whether retaining the target conversation improves the likelihood of the identical response. Results report `query_only - full_context` NLL and BPB gain, with response-token micro and per-example macro aggregation, sliced by needle count and evidence distance.

### Difference from standard MRCR

Standard OpenAI MRCR gives the model the complete conversation, samples a response, requires the nonce prefix in that response, and grades the generated text with a `SequenceMatcher` similarity score. This experiment instead teacher-forces the gold response and measures its token likelihood twice: once with the target conversation and once without it. The supplied prefix is not scored. The resulting paired NLL/BPB gain is a diagnostic of context use, not an official MRCR generation score, and should not be compared directly with published MRCR scores.

## Hypothesis or Goal

Context gain (`query_only - full_context`) should move from non-positive before extension to positive after 64K/262K adaptation. Fixed qk=1.57 comparisons isolate checkpoint adaptation; qk=1.75 is the deployable final arm.

### Links

- [OpenAI MRCR dataset and task description](https://huggingface.co/datasets/openai/mrcr/tree/f4c69fae7cf81f7ca26b9fee34b392a50f6b8a1d)
- [Research logbook](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/babf963076/.agents/logbooks/paired-mrcr-base-eval.md)
- [Implementation snapshot](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/commit/63027b4e72)
- [Final qk1.57 W&B](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/mrcr-67b-step157000-qk157-cap262144-two_shot-v464cp8ep4)
- [Final qk1.75 W&B](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/mrcr-67b-step157000-qk175-cap262144-two_shot-v464cp8ep4)

## Results

Context gain is `query_only - full_context`, so positive NLL or BPB gain is beneficial.

| Checkpoint | qk | NLL gain (95% CI) | BPB gain |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |

spillover_issues.author: rjpower
spillover_issues.body:
Some potential improvements we noticed during the hero run rollout.

scatter aggregation:
  - can you run a scatter aggregation step alongside the mappers? for each N map shards finished, read them in and reshuffle/merge the outputs by reduce shard. the inputs should be pre-sorted by target shard, so in theory this can be done with low-memory. this should reduce read traffic by a factor of ~N, and potentially eliminates the external sort we currently do entirely

datafusion as a loading api:
  - supports parquet reading & query push down
  - seems robust from our experience with finelog
  - trivializes a "lite" sql select only API
  - would be nice for library sharing across projects

mapper auto-tuning:
  - choose the number of mappers for the user based on heuristics or dynamically based on observations
  - we have many pipelines that run 10x too slow just because they have fewer mappers than needed
  - combine this with the scatter aggregation to avoid map/reduce shard blowup

better partial recovery:
  - allow recovering a partially complete run
  - for example the zephyr coordinator might write a state record once a minute recording all of the shard state
  - check for this when booting up and reuse it if the ids match

kv-store work scattering:
  - the kv store actors can be used in the some situations to split up imbalanced workloads
  - push the work to the kv store via compute functions

spillover_issues.author: wmoss
spillover_issues.body:
Iris controller restarts today are driven entirely by `iris cluster controller restart` (see `lib/iris/OPS.md`, `.agents/skills/restart-iris/`) — GCE clusters restart via SSH + `docker restart`, CoreWeave clusters via the Kubernetes API — not by Pulumi. This is an investigation, not a commitment to migrate: the restart flow has safety properties that a naive Pulumi resource-replace would break if not carried over deliberately.

Specifically: the controller keeps local SQLite state plus periodic GCS checkpoints, and restart takes a pre-restart checkpoint and writes a rollout record (image + matching checkpoint ref) so a failed health check can roll back atomically. DB migrations are forward-only and some are destructive, so restoring an old controller image without its paired pre-migration checkpoint breaks. Any Pulumi-driven approach needs to preserve this checkpoint-before-restart / paired-rollback behavior, e.g. by keeping restart-with-rollback as a wrapped CLI step (similar to how `iac.iris.service` wraps a CLI today) rather than modeling the controller as a plain replaceable resource.

comments.author: claude[bot]
comments.body:
🤖 Investigation, not a bug fix — no PR. Analysis below; handing off to a human for the migrate/don't-migrate call.

# Research

Confirmed the issue body against the code. `iris cluster controller restart` is a CLI-side choreography around a mechanical platform restart; the safety lives in the CLI, not in the platform primitive.

Forward deploy in [`cli/cluster.py:controller_restart` L1117-1215](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/iris/src/iris/cli/cluster.py#L1117-L1215): pre-deploy checkpoint (L1180) → build fresh images (L1182) → write `PENDING` rollout record (L1187) → `restart_controller` (L1199) → on health-check failure `_auto_rollback` to previous image + its pre-deploy checkpoint (L1202) → write `COMMITTED` (L1206). `--rollback` (L1148) reverts to the recorded previous image + checkpoint.

The rollout record is a small state machine in GCS remote state, not in any deploy tool's state; the restarted controller consumes `ROLLBACK_REQUESTED` once on boot and self-clears. Migrations are forward-only and some are destructive, so an old image must boot on its paired pre-migration checkpoint — this is why image and checkpoint are recorded as a pair.

**Relevant code**
- [`cli/cluster.py#L1117`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/iris/src/iris/cli/cluster.py#L1117) - restart/rollback choreography (checkpoint, record, restart, auto-rollback)
- [`controller/rollout.py`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/iris/src/iris/cluster/controller/rollout.py) - `RolloutPhase`/`RolloutRecord`, read/write in GCS remote state
- [`platforms/vm_lifecycle.py#L409`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/iris/src/iris/cluster/platforms/vm_lifecycle.py#L409) / [`k8s/controller.py#L517`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/iris/src/iris/cluster/platforms/k8s/controller.py#L517) - mechanical restart primitives (no safety logic)
- [`controller/migrations/`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/main/lib/iris/src/iris/cluster/controller/migrations) - forward-only, sometimes destructive
- [`iac/iris/service.py#L156-L164`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/infra/pulumi/src/iac/iris/service.py#L156-L164) - existing CLI-wrap template to reuse

# Proposed approach

Do **not** model the controller as a plain replaceable Pulumi resource. A resource-replace would tear down and recreate around the restart, bypassing the checkpoint/rollout-record choreography and losing atomic rollback on a bad deploy.

Instead reuse the pattern already in [`iac/iris/service.py`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/infra/pulumi/src/iac/iris/service.py) (and the sibling finelog migration in #7571): wrap `iris cluster controller restart` in a `command.local.Command` component whose `create`/`update` verb runs the restart CLI and whose `delete` is a no-op (or `stop`, deliberately). Key the resource on the controller image tag plus a code hash so a change triggers `update` = restart-with-rollback; a failed health check propagates as a Command error, and the CLI has already auto-rolled-back. The rollout record stays in GCS remote state so `--rollback` keeps working out-of-band from Pulumi state.

Open questions for the human owner:
- Is the goal declarative *drift correction* (Pulumi restarts when image drifts) or just *inventory* (record the controller in the stack without owning restarts)? The wrapper above gives the former; only the latter avoids Pulumi ever triggering a restart.
- How should a Pulumi `up` that fails its health check and auto-rolls-back report to the operator — hard resource failure, or success-with-warning after rollback?
- Interaction with the manual `restart-iris` skill / direct CLI runs: Pulumi must treat an out-of-band restart as convergent, not as drift to undo.

Scope is a new Pulumi component plus wiring — multi-file design work, so leaving implementation to a human per the migration effort in #7571/#7262.

comments.author: loom-oa-dev[bot]
comments.body:
🤖 Investigation result: move Iris controller operations under the shared deploy interface, with Pulumi invoking the existing migration-aware restart transaction. Do not make the controller VM or Kubernetes Deployment a plain replaceable Pulumi resource.

Effort: medium, 2026-08-24. I stopped after the current code, linked PRs, Echo history, and Pulumi documentation converged on the same boundary.

### Current Marin context

The new work changes the operator interface, but not Iris's state-safety requirement:

- [#8537](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/8537) provides one command tree for Pulumi applications. The executable merged there is `marin-deploy`, so the exact spelling today is `uv run marin-deploy ...`; adding a `deploy` script alias is independent of this design.
- [`controller restart`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/1936313ac7da5e1c4f08c0a1634e24cf66f4e772/lib/iris/src/iris/cli/cluster.py#L1263-L1532) resolves secrets, checkpoints the live controller, builds and pins images, writes `PENDING`, restarts in place, health-checks, and commits or restores the previous image plus checkpoint. The controller [consumes the rollback request once](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/1936313ac7da5e1c4f08c0a1634e24cf66f4e772/lib/iris/src/iris/cluster/controller/main.py#L51-L85).
- Pulumi [does not automatically roll back a failed update](https://www.pulumi.com/docs/support/faq/infrastructure/#automatic-rollbacks). Finelog therefore captures the active revision outside Pulumi, runs `pulumi up`, restores on failure, and refreshes state ([#7690](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/7690), [current implementation](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/1936313ac7da5e1c4f08c0a1634e24cf66f4e772/lib/finelog/src/finelog/deploy/_k8s.py#L390-L471)). Iris needs that recovery boundary and its additional checkpoint pairing.

### Recommended first migration

1. Add a separate `infra/iris` application project with one stack per controller cluster. This follows the repository rule that application deploy lifecycles stay outside the static `infra/pulumi` substrate project.
2. Add an Iris controller component backed by `command.local.Command`. Its `create` and `update` verbs run the existing `iris cluster controller restart`; removal has no stop/delete verb. Inputs include the cluster, reviewed config hash, working-tree hash, and an explicit deploy generation for a forced same-tree restart. Pulumi's command provider runs `update` when inputs/triggers change instead of replacing the resource ([provider contract](https://www.pulumi.com/registry/packages/command/api-docs/local/command/)).
3. Add service-specific commands:

   ```text
   uv run marin-deploy iris rollout <cluster>
   uv run marin-deploy iris rollout <cluster> --force
   uv run marin-deploy iris rollback <cluster>
   ```

   `rollback` must call the existing `--rollback` path and use the GCS rollout record. Pulumi history is not a substitute for the recorded image/checkpoint pair. The rollout record remains the recovery source of truth; Pulumi records which reviewed tree/config triggered the transaction.
4. Keep the existing fleet gates: clean/current tree preflight, one cluster at a time, baseline snapshot, five-minute verification, and smoke job. Do not add Iris to the parallel path-triggered deployment matrix in the first change. That matrix cannot currently stop the fleet at the first failed cluster, and GCE restarts also require per-user SSH access.

This stage gives Iris the shared `marin-deploy` UX and Pulumi update/audit surface while preserving the current transaction even when an operator runs `pulumi up` directly.

### Native-resource follow-up

A later CoreWeave-only stage can adopt the non-secret runtime objects into an application stack: ConfigMap, protected PVC, Recreate Deployment, Service, PDB, node-agent DaemonSet, LocalQueue, and priority classes. It should proceed only after the deploy driver is split into prepare/activate/finalize/rollback operations and these conditions are tested:

- no workload mutation before a fresh checkpoint and `PENDING` record;
- every activation or health failure restores the recorded image and checkpoint, waits for `ROLLED_BACK`, then refreshes Pulumi state;
- direct `pulumi up` cannot bypass preparation;
- secret values remain outside Pulumi state;
- controller storage is protected, and GCE application changes never replace the controller VM;
- manual break-glass rollback remains convergent with the next intentional rollout.

Confidence is high for the first migration. Native CoreWeave ownership is feasible with those gates, but it is a separate lifecycle refactor; GCE should continue using the in-place SSH restart mechanism behind the same command.

### Handoff

No PR was opened because this request was an investigation. The next decision is whether to implement the first migration as scoped above and track native CoreWeave resource ownership separately.

spillover_issues.author: penfever
spillover_issues.body:
The Evaldash Panel's default view ("Newest per benchmark (all cohorts)", filter `cohort: all`) still drops runs that violate a named eval policy. On 2026-11-25 the default Panel showed "292 run(s) excluded from this cohort". The default view should show every valid result. It should apply a policy's exclusions only when the user selects that policy's cohort.

Reproduce:
1. Open https://marina.oa.dev/evaldash/ (Panel tab) with no filters.
2. Leave Cohort at "Newest per benchmark (all cohorts)".
3. The banner reads "292 run(s) excluded from this cohort", and those runs contribute no cells.

Expected: with cohort "all", no run is excluded for policy violations. Each cell shows the newest valid result, whatever its cohort, under the existing "All cohorts may mix evaluation settings" warning. The policy-violation exclusions (and the PolicyRejections banner) apply only when a specific policy cohort is selected.

Cause: `_policy_rejections` in `infra/marina/apps/evaldash/metrics.py:228` drops every record with a non-empty `record_policy_violations(record)` (`lib/evalrecords/src/evalrecords/eval_policy.py:257`). It applies the cohort check `in_cohort(record, request)` but no check for the "all cohorts" selection. The Compare page uses the same rejection list (`ComparePage.vue:235`), so it needs the same rule.

Scope note: the coverage gate, smoke runs and failed or unscored runs are separate validity rules. They are not policy exclusions and stay as they are. Related: #9458, which covers policy conformance from trusted evidence.

Done when:
- The default Panel and Compare views (cohort "all") exclude no run for policy violations and show no "excluded from this cohort" banner for them.
- Selecting a named policy cohort still excludes and lists that policy's violating runs.
- A test in `infra/marina/apps/evaldash/tests/test_metrics.py` covers both cases.
