spillover_issues.author: dbuddha
spillover_issues.body:
Hi all, I'm Deepak, a Stanford student, and I've been working on this as my CS221 project. It started from Will's suggestion to begin with the Delphi seed repeats, and from his note in the Nov 2 standup (#11169) that, with loop variance this high, it would help to have documented expected variance so agents know what counts as a regression. Calvin also suggested in #data-mixing that we target fewer evals, possibly one that generalizes well, instead of a big aggregate, so I tested one version of that too. Everything here uses public data, and I'm happy to share more detail on any of it.

## Short version

I measured how much eval scores move between training seeds of the same recipe. I used DataDecide's per-question results (3 seeds per recipe), and the public Delphi seed triples at 1e21 and 1e22, which I scored with Marin's eval suite and the pinned stanford-crfm harness.

The part I think is most useful for Marin is that item-sampling SE is not a good stand-in for seed noise, and it misses in both directions. For soft metrics like gold log-prob or BPB, item SE usually understates seed noise, sometimes several times over. For accuracy it depends on the task: item SE overstates seed noise for HellaSwag and MMLU on DataDecide, and understates it for the DataDecide 10-task average. For Delphi MMLU 0-shot accuracy the ratio is about 1.3, which is within noise of 1 with three seeds. The ratio may also move with scale. For MMLU 0-shot log-prob on Delphi, seed SD is about 4x the item SE at 1e21 and about 1x at 1e22, though with three seeds per scale that change isn't significant (p about 0.1).

On Calvin's suggestion, picking a single eval by SNR went badly. The 10-task average ordered 82% of recipe pairs the same way as at 1B, and the highest-SNR single eval got 57%. The best single eval in hindsight tied the average, but it is the best of 20 and changes with the decision scale, and on Marin's swarms (comment below) the best single task in hindsight trails the aggregate.

I also tried to forecast seed noise as a power law in compute, and that did not work.

## Why this matters for the current gates

Several gates set thresholds from item SEs or fixed bands, and the ones that use seed replicates have only a few:

- The release tie rule in #10197 uses unpaired item SEs. There is an open question there about paired SEs. For picking one fixed release checkpoint, item SE may be the right noise. Seed noise matters when the call is about a recipe.
- Data Belay (#11582) uses 3 seeds per arm with a 1% floor, and suggests pooling the control's seed variance across rungs.
- The loop presets in #10740 compare against a few control replicates.
- #11177 notes that paired-item variance is unmeasured.
- #10804 notes that interval calibration for Mini840 and Micro210 is not established.
- Belay (#9451) uses a fixed 0.005 band.
- Ladder forecasts like #10753 seem to fit one run per rung, so seed noise at the small rungs would go straight into the extrapolation.

#5247 is the closest earlier work on choosing a useful set of evals. It measured noise from 10 repeat runs at 300M and ended on choosing, for each task, the smooth proxy with the highest SNR. Result 2 tests a different rule, keeping one eval chosen by SNR across all tasks, which is closer to the fewer-evals idea.

## What I measured

**DataDecide** (`allenai/DataDecide-eval-instances`, revision `23f3b2e`). 10 OLMES tasks, using each task's primary metric and the gold-choice log-prob per character. I used two subsets:

- Eval selection (Results 2 and 3): 24 of the 25 recipes, 3 seeds each, read at the last step that every recipe and seed shares: 150M at 37,500, 300M at 45,000 and 1B at 69,369. These are about 98% of training for the two smaller sizes, and final for 1B. I left out `dolma1.7-no-math-no-code`, because its 1B seed 4 only has a checkpoint at 57,500.
- Noise forecast and the DataDecide ratios (Results 1 and 4): 5 recipes (`c4`, `dclm-baseline`, `dolma1.7`, `falcon-with-cc`, `fineweb-edu`) at all five sizes, each read at the last step its three seeds share. For 530M and 750M that step is at 89% and 43% of the schedule.

**Delphi on Marin's suite.**

- Checkpoints: `delphi-1e21-3.4Bparams-46.3Btokens` and `delphi-1e22-9.7Bparams-160Btokens`, default seed plus seeds 42 and 62746.
- Tasks: `mmlu_sl_verb` 0-shot and 5-shot, and the `logprob_gsm8k_5shot` and `logprob_humaneval_10shot` configs from [`experiments/exp1337_eval_suite.py`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/f08afdb5ec98c742c06a5e72d9a987aa9db1e450/experiments/exp1337_eval_suite.py) (since removed from main in #6633).
- Harness: `stanford-crfm/lm-evaluation-harness@d5e3391f` with the HF backend on one H100, BF16 weights, batch size auto. I logged per-sample results.
- I recreated the two logprob tasks as YAML with the same fields as the suite, except that I requested perplexity instead of `bpb` so the harness would log each document's log-likelihood. I computed BPB per document from that log-likelihood and the target's bytes, which matches the suite's per-document mean.

**Delphi GSM8K rollouts.** The per-seed rollouts that `tatsu-lab/hinted-scaling-laws` (commit `c0490e5`) published: 256 problems for every seeded Delphi budget, with 32 rollouts per hint level and 64 unhinted. That repo has no license file, so I only report aggregates from it.

## Results

### 1. Seed noise vs item SE on Delphi

Each value is seed SD divided by item SE. Seed SD is taken across the three seeds, and item SE comes from the default seed (micro averages).

| Metric | 1e21 | 1e22 |
|---|---:|---:|
| MMLU 0-shot accuracy | 1.28 | 1.35 |
| MMLU 0-shot gold-choice log-prob | 4.10 | 1.03 |
| MMLU 5-shot accuracy | 0.71 | 0.69 |
| MMLU 5-shot gold-choice log-prob | 1.99 | 1.83 |
| GSM8K 5-shot BPB | 2.61 | 0.56 |
| HumanEval 10-shot BPB (see the fidelity note) | 0.05 | 1.02 |

DataDecide (the 5-recipe subset) shows a similar split. For accuracy on HellaSwag and MMLU, seed SD is 0.3x to 0.75x the item SE, but for BoolQ accuracy it is 4x to 9x. For gold log-prob on ARC-Easy, HellaSwag and MMLU it is 1.1x to 12x, and it is largest at 530M and 750M, whose checkpoints come before the end of the LR schedule. Across all 10 tasks, gold log-prob ranges from 0.3x (WinoGrande) to 88x (BoolQ).

So I don't think one rule of thumb works. An item-SE tie rule is on the cautious side for some accuracy metrics, too willing to call differences real for others, and too willing for most soft metrics. These ratios are exploratory, not part of a preregistered test.

### 2. Does one eval recover the winner? (Calvin's suggestion)

Setup: I picked a recipe using results at 300M (or 150M), and counted it correct if it matched the sign of the 3-seed mean macro accuracy at 1B, over all 276 recipe pairs. SNR is the spread of recipe means divided by the pooled seed SD, measured at 150M only. I wrote the plan down before computing any of these numbers.

| Decide at | Seeds per recipe | 10-task average | Highest-SNR single eval (HellaSwag gold log-prob) | Best single eval in hindsight |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---|
| 300M | 1 | 0.822 | 0.570 | CSQA accuracy, 0.819 |
| 300M | 3 | 0.848 | 0.569 | CSQA accuracy, 0.848 |
| 150M | 1 | 0.797 | 0.600 | OpenBookQA gold log-prob, 0.786 |
| 150M | 3 | 0.808 | 0.605 | CSQA accuracy, 0.815 |

At 300M with one seed per recipe, the bootstrap 95% interval for "single eval minus average" is -0.447 to -0.048. The interval resamples recipes, 2,000 draws. At 150M the intervals cross zero (-0.398 to +0.030 with one seed per recipe, -0.410 to +0.019 with three). PIQA accuracy actually points the wrong way (0.44).

HellaSwag gold log-prob separates recipes very consistently, but in a different order from the broad target. Every eval here runs on the same training runs, so the average adds eval compute but no extra runs. My read is that low noise alone isn't enough to pick one eval. CSQA accuracy tied the average here, but I only know that in hindsight, and it gets 0.73 when the decision is made at 150M.

One fair objection is that the 1B target is accuracy, which is noisy. So I also scored the same 300M picks (one seed per recipe) against smooth 1B targets. This check is exploratory:

| Picked at 300M | 1B average accuracy (target above) | 1B average gold log-prob | 1B HellaSwag gold log-prob |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| HellaSwag gold log-prob (highest SNR) | 0.570 | 0.510 | 0.941 |
| Average of the 10 gold log-probs | 0.844 | 0.844 | 0.466 |
| Average of the 10 accuracies | 0.822 | 0.779 | 0.435 |

The two broad 1B targets agree on 90% of pairs, and the smooth one doesn't rescue the single eval. HellaSwag gold log-prob tracks HellaSwag itself across scale (94%), so here the problem looks like breadth more than smoothness. On Marin's swarms some single tasks also reorder between rungs (comment below). Averaging the smooth proxies did best for both broad targets.

### 3. Tie rules on the aggregate

Decisions at 300M with one seed per recipe, on the 10-task average:

| Rule | Share of pairs it calls | Accuracy when it calls |
|---|---:|---:|
| Unpaired item-SE rule (1.96 x hypot of item SEs) | 0.75 | 0.886 |
| Fixed 1% relative band | 0.89 | 0.852 |
| Seed-calibrated: seed variance = 2.69 x item variance, fit at 150M only | 0.61 | 0.919 |

The seed-calibrated rule is the item-SE rule with the threshold widened by sqrt(2.69) = 1.64, so it is stricter by construction, and a higher hit rate on its calls is expected. It gets fewer pairs right overall (56% of all pairs vs 67%). The useful part is the 2.69 itself: on a fixed benchmark, a 1.96 item-SE threshold is only 1.2 seed SDs here, so under a normal approximation two equal recipes would be called different about 23% of the time instead of 5%.

### 4. Forecasting seed noise across scale (negative result)

I fit log seed variance as a power law in compute on the smaller sizes, and scored the forecast on held-out larger ones. On DataDecide (the 5-recipe subset, fit on 150M to 530M, 1B held out), it beat the best simple baseline in only 4 of 20 task and metric groups. A simpler rule did better there (seed variance as a fixed multiple of item variance), winning 11 of 20, though only 5 of 20 at 750M.

On the Delphi GSM8K rollouts, both lost to the best baseline at 1e21 and 1e22. Seed noise on the main hinted metric dropped from 2.8 points at 1e21 to 0.26 points at 1e22, while the power law expected it to keep growing. So I don't think a compute-only law is the right way to set thresholds per rung, at least with 3 seeds, and a ratio fit at one scale may not carry to another.

### Smaller things

- Scoring the same 1e21 default weights twice (first pass) gave identical per-question values, so eval nondeterminism isn't behind the seed differences.
- Between pairs of Delphi seeds, 39% to 65% of MMLU answers change, and correctness flips on 24% to 34% of questions.
- On MMLU 0-shot, a question that flips between seeds at 1e21 is only a little more likely to flip at 1e22 (0.49 vs 0.40, phi 0.10). This one is exploratory.
- As a sanity check, refitting Chinchilla Approach 2 on `delphi-blog-data` reproduces Delphi's published optimal model sizes within about 3%. Fit only up to 3e20, it predicts the released losses at 1e21, 1e22 and 1e23 within 0.3%.

## Fidelity against Marin's published default-seed numbers

I averaged every metric per subject, because that is what matches Marin's published numbers. The fork's group value does the same for `choice_logprob`, but weights accuracy by subject size (0.2700 at 1e21 and 0.4110 at 1e22), so its group accuracy won't match the blog at 1e22. Each pair is this run vs `delphi-blog-data`.

| Metric | 1e21 | 1e22 |
|---|---|---|
| MMLU 0-shot accuracy | 0.2703 vs 0.2710 | 0.4191 vs 0.4192 |
| MMLU 0-shot `choice_logprob` | -1.51430 vs -1.51440 | -1.29253 vs -1.29259 |
| MMLU 5-shot accuracy | 0.2783 vs 0.2751 | 0.4675 vs 0.4699 |
| MMLU 5-shot `choice_logprob` | -1.48028 vs -1.47965 | -1.21529 vs -1.21474 |
| GSM8K 5-shot BPB | 0.5637 vs 0.5631 | 0.4391 vs 0.4384 |
| HumanEval 10-shot BPB | 0.6147 vs 0.5195 | 0.4819 vs 0.4136 |

HumanEval doesn't match, and I haven't found why yet. It isn't truncation: the longest context is 2,669 tokens. GSM8K matches with the same BPB formula. If anyone knows how the HumanEval numbers in the Delphi post were produced (backend, tokenization of the solution, few-shot source), I'd love to fix it. Until then I'm treating the HumanEval rows as this harness only.

## Evidence and setup

- Command for the first pass: `lm_eval --model hf --model_args pretrained=<checkpoint>,dtype=bfloat16 --tasks mmlu_sl_verb,logprob_gsm8k_5shot,logprob_humaneval_10shot --include_path <tasks dir> --batch_size auto --log_samples --output_path <out>`. The 5-shot pass used `--tasks mmlu_sl_verb --num_fewshot 5`.
- Versions: lm-eval 0.4.9.1 from the fork, transformers 4.57.6, datasets 3.6.0, on the `runpod/pytorch:1.0.2-cu1281-torch280-ubuntu2404` image with one H100 80GB.
- Delphi revisions:
  - 1e21: `37bd7d2`, `cf238a2` (seed 42), `63f48f1` (seed 62746).
  - 1e22: `8ac3229`, `fb30c1b` (seed 42), `fcc5ce0` (seed 62746).
  - Blog data: `78f8e0c`.
- Cost: 13 runs (6 checkpoints x 2 passes, plus one A/A repeat) in 4.36 billed H100-hours, including installs and downloads.
  - A 3.4B first pass took about 7 minutes of eval time.
  - MMLU 5-shot is 41.9M tokens per checkpoint, and 0-shot is 7.3M.
- Process: I committed the plans for the forecast (Result 4) and the eval selection (Results 2 and 3) before scoring the held-out data. The ratio tables, the target check in Result 2 and the flip analysis are exploratory. I can share the notes, the per-question outputs and the scripts.

## Limits

- Only 3 seeds per configuration, so a single seed SD is uncertain by roughly 0.5x to 6x (95%), and I lean on pooling across recipes and metrics.
- Two families (OLMo-style DataDecide up to 1B, and Delphi). Delphi has no recipe pairs, so the decision-accuracy results come from DataDecide only.
- These are pretraining log-likelihood evals. Loop evals generate answers, and an earlier version of the #10740 description reported 210 of 1,500 task scores changing between two greedy passes of the same weights, so the numbers here may not carry over. The method should.
- The 1e21 W&B configs set trainer seeds 0, 42 and 62746 with `data_seed` null, and Levanter then derives the data order from the trainer seed. So each seed changes both initialization and data order, and I can't say which one drives the noise. The 1e21 default run also used a different code commit (`de20b33`) from the two seed runs (`67099b9`). I haven't checked the 1e22 configs.

## Asks

- **@Calvin-Xu**: to test the eval-selection result on Marin's own mixtures, I'd need the same mixtures run at a small and a larger rung with the same evals. The public `grug-moe-mix-swarm` has 10 seed repeats of a proportional mix at d512, and 10 runs of a proportional mix at d768 (their names show different loader settings too), but the two use different stores, and I couldn't match any d512 design to a d768 one. Do you know if a two-rung set like that exists?
- **@penfever**: would a per-metric seed-noise table be useful for the tie rule in #10197, maybe with a separate threshold for soft metrics? I realize it matters more for recipe calls than for picking a fixed release checkpoint.
- **@Helw150** and **@RohithKuditipudi**: the 20 seed checkpoints from #10555 (blocked by #10758), or just their per-question eval outputs, would let me fit noise for multiple-choice metrics across eleven budgets instead of two. Even 3e19 and 3e20 would help.
- And if anyone is already looking at seed noise on the Delphi ladder, I'd really like to compare notes rather than duplicate it

Thanks for reading, and for putting all of this out in the open

_Edited Nov 21: fixed the accuracy claim (item SE understates seed noise for some accuracy metrics too), described the 5-recipe DataDecide subset, and corrected the rollout counts, the budget count, the MMLU aggregation note, the Result 3 reading and two links. Added #10753, the #5247 context and an exploratory target check in Result 2._

_Edited Nov 26: corrected how I described #5247 (it picks a smooth proxy per task), softened the hindsight-eval and Delphi-ratio claims, which three seeds can't support, added the 150M intervals, tightened the #10804 and #10753 descriptions, and noted the one field I changed in the task configs. The swarm results are in the comment below._

comments.author: Calvin-Xu
comments.body:
> Do you know if a two-rung set like that exists?

Our data mixing swarms are probably useful:

> The same 280 mixtures over 39 data buckets (238 sampled designs, 39 single-bucket removals, and 3 baselines) were trained at three settings: Llama 160M/1.2B, Llama 200M/6B, and Qwen3 360M/1.6B (about 3e18 FLOPs). Each setting also has 10 repeats of the proportional mixture. Every run has BPB on the same 58 tasks: the 7 Uncheatable Eval corpora and the 51 OlmoBaseEval Easy tasks.
> 
> | Setting | Repeat SD, Uncheatable BPB | Repeat SD, OBE Easy mean BPB | Spearman with 360M/1.6B (Uncheatable / OBE Easy) |
> |---|---:|---:|---:|
> | Llama 160M/1.2B | 0.0011 | 0.0054 | 0.92 / 0.85 |
> | Llama 200M/6B | 0.0012 | 0.0035 | 0.62 / 0.55 |
> | Qwen3 360M/1.6B | 0.0009 | 0.0038 | |
> 
> Repeat SDs come from the 10 proportional repeats; the Spearman correlations are over the 238 sampled designs.
> 
> The 871 checkpoints are public on Hugging Face as `Calvin-Xu/mariner-swarm-llama-160m-1p2b`, `Calvin-Xu/mariner-swarm-llama-200m-6b`, and `Calvin-Xu/mariner-swarm-qwen3-360m-1p6b`.

The same dataset has a ladder with more scales and fewer recipes: proportional, UniMax, and MARINER's and Olmix's proposals at 3e18, 2e19, 3e20, and 1e21 FLOPs, though only proportional at 3e18 have seed repeats.

comments.author: dbuddha
comments.body:
Thanks @Calvin-Xu for sharing those!! I committed the test plan before opening any BPB columns and then ran it once. It decides on Llama 160M/1.2B and scores against Llama 200M/6B over the 238 sampled mixtures, one run each. 200M/6B has 1.3x the parameters, 5x the tokens and half the peak learning rate, so it tests repetition as much as scale. A rule gets a pair right if it orders the two mixtures the same way 200M/6B does, and a task's SNR is its SD across the 238 designs over its SD across the 10 proportional repeats at 160M. The numbers below are decision accuracy, the share of the 28,203 pairs a rule gets right, so 0.5 is a coin flip.

| Picked at 160M/1.2B | Decision accuracy against OBE Easy mean BPB at 200M/6B | Decision accuracy against Uncheatable BPB at 200M/6B |
|---|---:|---:|
| The target's own aggregate | 0.811 | 0.822 |
| Highest-SNR single task | 0.520 (SciQ, SNR 22.8) | 0.513 (BBC News, SNR 24.0) |
| Mean of the 5 highest-SNR tasks | 0.599 | |
| Best single task in hindsight | 0.784 (MT-MBPP R) | 0.771 (GitHub Python) |

On OBE Easy the highest-SNR task trails the aggregate by 29 points of decision accuracy, with a bootstrap 95% interval of -34 to -24 when I resample mixtures. The gap holds when the aggregate and the target share no tasks; with the 51 OBE Easy tasks split in half, one half at 160M against the other half at 200M/6B, it's 0.776 against 0.529. Noise in the target doesn't explain it either, since on the pairs that are clearly apart at 200M/6B (more than 3 SDs of a two-run difference) the aggregate goes up to 0.883 and SciQ stays at 0.523. Your `fits_reliability` SNRs are on the Qwen3 swarm over the 280 fit runs, so they differ from my 160M ones, and they put HellaSwag first among the OBE Easy tasks. As a lone pick HellaSwag gets 0.518, but your SNR-threshold subsets hold up well; the means of the SNR≥2, ≥5 and ≥8 tasks (49, 32 and 17 tasks) get 0.809, 0.799 and 0.773, close to the full aggregate. I reproduced your Spearman table and repeat SDs exactly, so I think we're reading the data the same way.

The ladder agrees, though it's an easy test; 14 of the 15 pairs are already more than 2 SDs apart at 3e18. The 3e18 aggregate orders all 15 the same way as 1e21, SciQ gets 7 and HellaSwag gets 1, and the MARINER and Olmix proposals were fit to those aggregates, so the aggregate has a head start there.

The rest I looked at after the planned test, so it's exploratory. A lot of the single-task gap is breadth; even at the same rung, SciQ orders only about 0.6 of pairs the same way as the 51-task average. Small-rung SNR doesn't say much about which tasks transfer to that average; across the 51 tasks its rank correlation with decision accuracy is 0.06 (0.28 against each task's own 200M/6B ranking), and SciQ and HellaSwag are near the bottom while the median task gets 0.69. SciQ doesn't agree with itself across the two rungs either; at 160M it orders only 0.57 of pairs the same way as SciQ at 200M/6B, while HellaSwag log-prob did that at 0.94 on DataDecide. My guess is that the 6B runs repeat the small buckets more and that shifts single tasks around, but I haven't checked it yet. The other pairings of your swarms look the same, with the aggregate against SciQ at 0.837 against 0.612 from 160M to Qwen3 360M and 0.697 against 0.494 from Qwen3 360M to 200M/6B.

So on your mixtures, as on DataDecide, one task picked for low noise doesn't stand in for the average of all the BPBs (which is also the mean of log-probs here), while SNR-filtered averages like yours stay close to it. If we want fewer evals, filtering by SNR inside an average looks safe, and going down to one or two tasks probably needs them picked by agreement with a larger rung, which I haven't tested. Happy to share the plan and scripts if that's useful.

@Helw150, your GDsuite results on the same Delphi seed triples line up with the item-SE point in the original post; on its two-choice tasks the median seed SD is about 9 to 10 times the binomial item SE at both 1e21 and 1e22 (17 and 21 tasks, ranging from 0.6x to 82x), though the items are templated, so the binomial SE may be too small and I can't size that without the raw files. The README mentions per-item `raw/` files and I think only `summary.jsonl` made it to the Hub, so if those are easy to add for the six seed checkpoints I could run the paired version of this on them too. For the extra seeds, I know the uploads would need input/help based on #10758 (cc @RohithKuditipudi). If per-question eval outputs from those runs are easier to share than the weights, they'd already cover what I need here

_Edits: labeled the table (the numbers are decision accuracy, not SNR), described your SNR table and subsets properly, added the breadth, rung and ladder caveats, and stated the GDsuite ratio as a median._

spillover_issues.author: penfever
spillover_issues.body:
### Summary
An unparseable candidate must grade 0, failing closed, and never crash the grader into an infrastructure failure. A live attempt shows the crash class still reaching production through a shipped grader: `/tests/grade.py` exited 1 with reward NULL and the attempt typed `GRADER_INFRASTRUCTURE_FAILURE` because `reasoning_gym.arithmetic.prime_factorization._normalize_answer` raised `ValueError` from `int()` on a prose candidate.

### Observed failure
- Attempt: job 8878689 (difficulty Small solver). Reward: NULL. Verdict type: `GRADER_INFRASTRUCTURE_FAILURE`.
- Mechanism: the pinned scorer's `_normalize_answer` (`reasoning_gym/arithmetic/prime_factorization.py` L55) does `int(factor.strip())` over the reply's `×`-separated factors; prose raises `ValueError: invalid literal for int()`. The task's `/tests/grade.py` does not catch it, so the grader exits nonzero and the attempt is scored as infrastructure failure instead of reward 0.0.

### Current main already fails closed (verified 2026-11-24)
Every live grading path routes scorer calls through `verifyit.modes.grade_reasoning_gym._score_candidate`, which catches `MALFORMED_REPLY_ERRORS` (including `ValueError`) and scores 0.0 while checking the entry's own answer still earns its reward, and the generated grade scripts (`reasoning_gym_grade.py`, Nemotron Ultra `reasoning_gym_grade.py`) call that function. Empirically on main `e1742c045`/`3279c897a4`: a prose `prime_factorization` candidate scores `0.0`, an empty one `0.01` (the scorer's own contract), the valid answer `1.0`. Behavior tests exist: `test_prime_factorization_prose_scores_zero_and_keeps_numeric_rewards`, `test_prime_factorization_bad_reference_is_an_invalid_task`. The guards landed in #11516 (2026-11-15) and #11937 (2026-11-21).

### Diagnosis
The failing job's shipped `/tests/grade.py` predates those guards — a deployed task package built from an earlier main. Frozen packages do not pick up scorer fixes until re-versioned.

### Asks
1. Identify the task package and version job 8878689 ran, confirm its `grade.py` predates the guards, and re-version the affected frozen selection so its grader picks up the fail-closed scorer.
2. A code-level defense at the last line of defense (weaverbot draft PR requested on this issue): the generated Reasoning Gym grade scripts should print `0.0` and exit 0 when the scorer raises on an unparseable candidate — verifying the entry's own answer still scores, so a broken entry stays an error — so a rebuilt package can never type an unparseable candidate `GRADER_INFRASTRUCTURE_FAILURE`, whatever exception a current or future scorer raises. Behavior tests: a prose candidate prints 0.0 with exit code 0, and a valid answer prints its real score.

Related: #11937 (malformed replies → 0.0 on main), #11990 (graded replies setting their own reward, fixed), #11516 (prime factors scored zero).
